,Progressive Conservative,,Gordon Francis Higgins,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=54481bbe-cafa-4aa9-823c-1bacb309f25f&Language=E&Section=ALL
1734279,ca.proc.d.1953-05-06.7.2,1953-05-06,52856d3c-42ed-4a84-9d56-17dfff0a98d5,ca.m.5949,Mr. Benidickson:,Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Transport,NEWFOUNDLAND HARBOURS,,,Boundary limits of a number of harbour beds in Newfoundland, which became the property of the crown in right of Canada under the terms of union of Newfoundland with Canada, have been suggested, and the matter now rests with the government of the province of Newfoundland which, it is understood, has referred it to the attorney general of Newfoundland for examination and report.

The management of certain harbours in Newfoundland was entrusted to harbour boards established by legislation, which legislation continues in force after the date of union, and under the terms of union, is now administered by the Minister of Transport.
Questions

These harbour boards have been permitted to exercise their functions until it is determined which boards are to be replaced by harbour masters, under the Canada Shipping Act, 1934, and which boards are to operate as harbour commissioners under new acts of incorporation. The harbour of Goose Bay has been proclaimed under the Canada Shipping Act, 1934, and a harbour master has been assigned there to enforce the regulations pertinent to public harbours.

St. Laurent (Prime Minister) moved:,Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council,BUSINESS OF THE HOUSE,"SITTING ON SATURDAY, MAY 9",,"That on Saturday, May 9, 1953, the sittings of the house shall in every respect be under the same rules as are now provided for other days under the special order passed on Thursday, April 2, 1953, and the order of business and procedure shall be the same as for Thursdays.

Fulton (Kamloops):,,BUSINESS OF THE HOUSE,SITTING ON SATURDAY, MAY 9",,"Mr. Speaker, before this motion is adopted I think the house is entitled to ask for an assurance from the Prime Minister with respect to one matter particularly. Although the motion provides that the order of business and procedure shall be the same as for Thursdays, we might have an undertaking, rather than an amendment, that questions will be called first. I beg your pardon, Mr. Speaker, the point is not that they will be called first; rather, the assurance I am after is that some of the questions which have been standing on the order paper for an extreme length of time will be answered.

I point out to you that question No. 1 has been on the order paper since February 25, two and a half months. Question No. 6 has been on the order paper since March 3, and question No. 12 has been on the order paper since March 23. Those are questions standing in my name and there are, in the names of other hon. members, others which have been standing since March 2, March 6, March 9, and so on. I would first like to protest against the length of time which has passed without these questions being

answered; and secondly, I would ask for an assurance that these questions will be answered before this session closes. I would ask that the question passed today as an order for return-question No. 6, which has been standing on the order paper since March 3-also be dealt with and the return brought down before the close of the session.

,Progressive Conservative,,Edmund Davie Fulton,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=bd7064c6-90b2-4e0a-9a8f-1c4d781bb30e&Language=E&Section=ALL
1734307,ca.proc.d.1953-05-06.12.1.3,1953-05-06,dcd2258a-b8c3-4099-bffb-7b24cce8341e,ca.m.9761,Mr. St. Laurent:,Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council,BUSINESS OF THE HOUSE,SITTING ON SATURDAY, MAY 9",,"I think it would be quite proper to have it agreed that questions might be called on Saturday at the appropriate time, but it is quite impossible to give the assurance asked for by the hon. member. I can give the hon. member the assurance that there was no intentional delay in dealing with any of these questions. He will recognize, as most members do, that there has been more work imposed upon the departments with respect to preparing answers and returns during this session than during any previous session I can remember. The work has been done just as expeditiously as it could be done by the staffs in the offices.
Everything that can be produced will be produced, but I cannot give assurance as to how much further time may be required to obtain the information that is sought.

Mutch (Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Veterans Affairs):,Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Veterans Affairs,ARMED FORCES,ELIGIBILITY OF KOREAN WAR VETERANS FOR BENEVOLENT OR WELFARE FUND ASSISTANCE,,Mr. Speaker, on Monday last the hon. member for Nanaimo (Mr. Pearkes) asked the following question:
Are Korean army veterans who have not had service in world war II eligible for assistance under the army welfare fund?
I promised at that time to secure an answer for him, and I now propose to give it.

The army benevolent fund was established by act of parliament to administer funds remaining from canteen operations during world war II. It provides assistance for veterans who served in the Canadian army during world war II and who may or may not be still serving. It also provides assistance for the dependents of these veterans or the former dependents of such veterans who have died.

The Canadian army welfare fund became available on April 1, 1953, and is being administered by the army benevolent fund on behalf of a board of directors. Assistance can be provided only for a person who is
Inquiries of the Ministry serving in the Canadian army, regardless of whether or not he served in world war II.

Owing to the limited funds available, the directors of the Canadian army welfare fund have not found it possible to extend this assistance to ex-members of the army, except that where a soldier dies, who had service in Korea, assistance will be available for a period of twelve months.

In the cases of veterans who require assistance but are not entitled to the Canadian army welfare fund assistance, the welfare officer does his best to obtain help through community resources, such as service clubs, Canadian Legion branches, army and navy branches, and such organizations as make it a practice to assist people in distress. A few of our district offices have at their disposal small trust funds, from which limited assistance can be provided.

The possibility of extending the scope of the Canadian army welfare fund to cover veterans who served in Korea is being discussed between the Department of Veterans Affairs and the Department of National Defence.

,Liberal,,Leslie Alexander Mutch,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=96d3f989-75c3-41f6-9e25-2d6cd12ef0a3&Language=E&Section=ALL

assistant a question about his statement. Does he mean that Korean army veterans do not have the same access to a benevolent fund as Korean navy veterans and Korean air force veterans have?

,Progressive Conservative,,Howard Charles Green,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=6dec82d6-fab3-438b-b40f-c7720a93d8c1&Language=E&Section=ALL
1734314,ca.proc.d.1953-05-06.13.1.4,1953-05-06,96d3f989-75c3-41f6-9e25-2d6cd12ef0a3,ca.m.7482,Mr. Mutch:,Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Veterans Affairs,ARMED FORCES,ELIGIBILITY OF KOREAN WAR VETERANS FOR BENEVOLENT OR WELFARE FUND ASSISTANCE,,Mr. Speaker, as the hon.

gentleman knows, the three benevolent funds-that is, the army, navy and air force benevolent funds-are separately set up and separately administered. In the case of the army benevolent fund there is no provision for extending benefits to serving personnel unless they served in world war II. That provision does not apply, I understand, to the other funds which continue to accept contributions from serving personnel.

,,,Some hon. Members:,
1734335,ca.proc.d.1953-05-06.16.3,1953-05-06,647c88fa-1673-4147-88b3-b42105bc54e3,ca.m.2918,Mr. Claxton:,Minister of National Defence,ANNOUNCEMENT OF ARRANGEMENTS FOR TRANSPORTING FILMS TO CANADA,,,The announcement is in connection with flying out to Canada of

telerecordings of the coronation. Arrangements have been completed with the air ministry and the British Broadcasting Corporation on the one hand, and the Royal Canadian Air Force and the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation on the other, whereby films will be flown by helicopter from the centre of London to Weald airport and flown out by Royal Air Force Canberra jet planes to Goose Bay. There they will be picked up by R.C.A.F. CF-100 aircraft and flown to Montreal. This arrangement has been worked out by the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation, and will provide television films, not only for the corporation but for five United States networks. They are the American Broadcasting System, the Columbia Broadcasting System, the National Broadcasting Company, Dumont and the Mutual Broadcasting System and one television news agency, U P Movietone.

These flights will, of course, be dependent on the weather, but they are timed so that delivery of the films at Montreal should take place at 4 p.m., 5.30 p.m. and 8.30 p.m. local daylight saving time. This would permit these films being shown in Montreal and Toronto, and would also permit their use for other purposes, broadcast and the like, within a few hours after the coronation itself takes place in London. It should permit also of their general dissemination throughout the United States through the arrangements initiated by the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation and carried out through the co-operation of the R.A.F. and the British Broadcasting Corporation, for which we are very grateful indeed.

,Liberal,,Brooke Claxton,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=647c88fa-1673-4147-88b3-b42105bc54e3&Language=E&Section=ALL

Herridge (Kootenay West):,,UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE,PAYMENT TO INSURED PERSONS BECOMING,INCAPACITATED THROUGH ILLNESS OR INJURY,Labour organizations, members of this group and other members in this house, during recent years in particular, have urged an amendment to the act to provide for benefits for those who are taken ill while in receipt of benefits. 1734360,ca.proc.d.1953-05-06.20.1.1.4,1953-05-06,103e48f0-b6bb-43eb-9c06-7ceffaf3ea78,ca.m.7989,Mr. Stanley Knowles (Winnipeg North Centre):,Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation,UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE,PAYMENT TO INSURED PERSONS BECOMING,INCAPACITATED THROUGH ILLNESS OR INJURY,As has been indicated by the two members who have already spoken this morning, Mr. Speaker, and as was indicated by those who spoke on this matter when it was at the resolution stage, this bill is a welcome piece of legislation. As has been stated already, it covers a point which has been raised in the house repeatedly, and we are glad that point at least is being covered.

However, Mr. Speaker, I feel that before the bill passes we should take this opportunity of indicating the further steps that have been necessary for a long time, but which will be even more necessary after this bill becomes law. As I said the other day when we were in committee of the whole on the resolution preceding this bill, the benefit to be provided under this legislation can be called a form of sickness benefit. I realize that technically that is not the correct name to apply to it. Technically speaking

Unemployment Insurance Act what will happen when this bill becomes law is that an insured worker, who has already started drawing unemployment insurance benefits because he is off work due to the fact that there was no work for him, will, when he is taken sick, be entitled to continue drawing these unemployment insurance benefits. Technically speaking, therefore, that sick or injured worker will be drawing unemployment insurance benefits. But I think we are justified in saying that it is the beginning of a form of sickness benefits, because to that extent, limited though it may be, we will have workers who are at home because of illness or injury drawing benefits out of a fund to which they have contributed.

As I suggested the other day this is a step from which there is no turning back. In common with the position taken by the labour congresses of this country, I urge upon the government the necessity of going further and extending this principle of sickness benefits to all workers covered by the unemployment insurance fund. In introducing this legislation the other day the minister made an oblique reference to the representations of the labour congress. I should like to draw to his attention a partial report of these representations which is contained in the most recent issue of the Labour Gazette, the issue for April, 1953. This is of course put out by the minister's own department. I find, for example on page 532 of this issue, included in a summary of the brief presented to the cabinet this year by the trades and labour congress of Canada, these interesting sentences:
The major change in the act requested by the delegation was the extension of the act to provide benefits to workers who are out of work because of illness.

In the TLC's view, administration of such a provision could be carried out by the present unemployment insurance commission. The provision would apply to the same employees now covered by the act; the system of contributions and benefits would be similar; the benefits would be paid to insured employees when sickness resulted in loss of earnings, on presentation of a doctor's certificate.
Those who are unemployed through sickness should receive benefits as a right,"" Mr. Bengough emphasized in a departure from his prepared text, ""and there should be no suggestion of any means test.""

That summary in the Labour Gazette is a faithful and fair report of one section of the brief from the trades and labour congress of Canada submitted to the government this year. It can be found on pages 12 and 13 of that brief.
Then over on page 537 of the same issue of the Labour Gazette, one finds references to the brief presented by the Canadian
congress of labour under the heading ""unemployment insurance"". There are two paragraphs I should like to place on the record. The first one reads as follows:

Reiterating its assertion that the unemployment insurance fund is over-funded, the congress prophesied a balance of a billion dollars in the near future if the present rate of employment is maintained. There is room for substantial improvements to the act without the need for further contributions, it said.
A little bit further down on the same page we find this:

The time has come, the brief stated, to introduce a sickness disability scheme to protect workers against loss of income during illness. Such a scheme, it suggested, could supplement unemployment insurance, be administered by the commission and be financed in part out of the ""large balance"" in the unemployment insurance fund.

Similarly on page 546 there appears a report of the representations of the transportation brotherhoods. I find that there are six improvements to the Unemployment Insurance Act which the brotherhoods suggest, and the last one reads as follows: . . . sickness disability insurance for all insured workers.

In other words, Mr. Speaker, this bill we now have before us, while welcomed by all of us in the house and by organized labour, is after all but a step in the direction of what the labour congresses asked for at the time they met the government this year. I suggest that this legislation should be looked upon as merely the beginning, merely as establishing the principle of the right of insured workers-workers who are contributing to a fund-to receive benefits in time of illness. They will be receiving these sickness benefits under this legislation but they will be receiving them not really by virtue of the fact that they are sick but rather by virtue of the fact that they are unemployed, that they started to draw their unemployment insurance benefits and then took ill while drawing those benefits.

I think the government is aware of the fact that this legislation will force action on the broader question; and that situation will come about because of some of the difficulties the government will run into in administering this scheme. ,Progressive Conservative,,Donald Methuen Fleming,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=5b04fb13-968f-4dac-80f6-3b569378e120&Language=E&Section=ALL
1734371,ca.proc.d.1953-05-06.20.1.1.15,1953-05-06,62287d4a-32a2-4734-a1b3-18cce52da443,ca.m.5390,Mr. Clarence Gillis (Cape Breton South):,,UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE,PAYMENT TO INSURED PERSONS BECOMING,INCAPACITATED THROUGH ILLNESS OR INJURY,Mr. Speaker, there are one or two things I should like to say about this bill. We welcome it as far as it goes. However, it certainly does not go far enough to suit me.
During the last discussion we had on unemployment insurance I brought to the

Unemployment Insurance Act minister's attention a matter which dovetails fairly realistically into this amendment but which is not covered. I pointed out to the minister the position of the employees of the Dominion Steel and Coal Corporation. They pay into a sickness benefit fund. That is a form of insurance that protects them against sickness. The employment in which they are engaged is heavy employment. A man may be too ill to carry out that type of heavy work, and so he is unemployed. But hir doctor tells him that he is in a position where his health will permit him to take lighter work. Under those circumstances that man, in my opinion, is legitimately entitled to apply for unemployment insurance. But if he does he immediately places himself in the position of severing his connection with the coal or steel company. Their attitude is that when you apply for unemployment insurance you automatically sever your connection with them, and the individual in turn not only loses his employment but he also loses his pension rights, because he has pension rights with that company. It has been a matter of controversy between the unions and the companies, both coal and steel, for some time. I drew that to the minister's attention, and the minister suggested that his department might have a talk with the coal and steel company on that particular point. This amendment certainly does not cover it.

I believe an employee in the circumstances that I have described is paying for insurance to protect him against sickness. He is legitimately entitled to draw insurance because he has paid for it. On the other hand, if he is not physically able to mine coal or to carry on heavy work in the steel plant but is able to engage in some other kind of employment that he might secure through the employment offices, he is legitimately entitled to collect his unemployment insurance, because he is paying for that also, and is capable of taking some type of work. That is not covered by this amendment. I am merely bringing that to the minister's attention again so that he can do something about it in the future. I think that type of case is being pretty badly discriminated against, not altogether by the government in the regulations but by the attitude of the company in the matter of employment and pension rights.

The second point that I should like to bring to the minister's attention-and it is not a new one-has to do with the discrimination practised against married women under regulation 5A. This goes back to the matter of illness. I have brought several cases to the minister's attention, or to the attention of the department, and I have argued

some of these cases before the board of referees and have even taken one to the umpire in Ottawa without getting any redress. I still get complaints. The difficulty appears to be that in a majority of the cases, so far as the young married women are concerned, they have no knowledge of the regulations. They are unorganized and they have no one to advise them in the matter until they get sick.

The last complaint I received was pretty bad. A girl was employed in a clerical capacity for ten years. She paid unemployment insurance during that time. She got married. She did not take any time off to get married; she continued on in her employment for some considerable time. Under regulation 5A, a young girl who is employed and wants to get married must take a separation from her employer and then re-hire and be employed for at least sixty days either in that employment or in some other. Why force a girl to discontinue her employment? Why force her to take separation because she wants to get married? Under the regulations they do. In this particular case she continued her employment for some considerable time. Then she carried out the instructions of the Good Book and did her share in populating the world. When that time arrived she took her separation from employment, not knowing anything about regulation 5A. Remember, this girl is ill within the meaning of the present regulations, except that she did not establish a benefit year. She makes her application for unemployment insurance. The unemployment insurance officer tells her that he cannot take an application from her; she is not entitled to unemployment insurance. She writes to the district office and they tell her: Well, you can appeal but there is no use your appealing; the board of referees will turn you down anyway under this regulation.

The point raised by the hon. member for St. John's West is a very difficult one; but it will be interpreted and dealt with in a liberal fashion-and the hon. member may use a large ""L"" or a small ""1"", whichever he wishes.

I am sure the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre realizes full well that under the terms of the amendment, which uses the expression ""no person who has become entitled to receive benefit"", there has to be a fixed date or a cut-off line somewhere. He will understand that, as in other measures, there are bound to be cases which, on the surface, do seem inequitable. However, we will deal with them as best we can. That is one factor which received a great deal of consideration at the time the amendment was under discussion.

Another point was touched upon by the hon. member for Hamilton West. It has to do with the availability of suitable work for an unemployed worker when he becomes sick. On that point I shall make a brief and carefully prepared statement. As is evident, the amendment has to do with section 27 of the act. That section contains three basic conditions precedent to the payment of benefit. These three conditions must be met for every day the benefit is paid. They are, of course: (a) that a person must be unemployed; (b) that he must be capable of and available for work; and (c) unable to obtain suitable employment.

The first of these, as I have indicated, is that the claimant must be unemployed, and the second and third are as I have stated them. The amendment modifies the second condition and allows the payment of benefits while he is incapacitated by reason of illness, injury or quarantine. The two other conditions, namely, that he must be unemployed and unable to obtain suitable employment, remain exactly as they were. The claimant must still prove that he is unemployed and he must still prove that he is unable to obtain suitable employment. When a job is offered to a claimant he will not be disqualified if he proves that he is genuinely ill. But if he fails to prove that he is ill, he will then be disqualified under the normal procedure of the act.
I am sure that the work test that was and is still in the act will be used by the

commission in a judicious manner in order to prevent any abuses of the fund. Generally I am quite confident that the insured population will not abuse their rights under the amendment to the act. On the other hand, the commission will apply the extensions fairly and generally and in a humane manner but will stand ready to use its powers to prevent any unwarranted claims on the fund.

I realize that the statement I have made is in general terms. Frankly, I would rather at this stage not be drawn into attempting to state what will be done in the given cases of John Smith or Bill Brown. The commis sion and its advisers have given a great deal of thought to the preparation of this amendment and they are exceedingly anxious that they be given a little time, not only in which to give more thought to these matters but in order to get directives in such shape that they may be placed in the hands of the 200 offices across the country so that the amendments may be put into operation as quickly and as uniformly as possible from one end of the country to the other. That explains why it is provided that the amendments shall come into force at a time to be set by the governor in council. I can assure the committee that that time will be made just as early as possible.

1734402,ca.proc.d.1953-05-06.21.1,1953-05-06,5b04fb13-968f-4dac-80f6-3b569378e120,ca.m.5224,Mr. Donald M. Fleming (Eglinton):,,UNITED STATES RESTRICTIONS,,,Mr. Speaker, there is a matter of some importance

U.S. Trade Restrictions that I should like to raise at this point. I shall endeavour to be brief, but I would not wish the brevity of my remarks to be interpreted as reflecting upon the importance of the matter. As I conceive it, it is a matter of very great importance.

I believe the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) leaves tomorrow for a meeting in Washington with President Eisenhower in response to an invitation from the United States president. I think all hon. members are glad indeed that President Eisenhower has invited the Prime Minister to this conference and that the Prime Minister has chosen to accept the invitation. Canada and the United States are the best neighbours in the world, but the fact that we are the best neighbours does not mean that there are not matters of mutual interest and high importance that must be discussed from time to time. I think that all hon. members will desire that these present discussions which will continue during the balance of the week will be fruitful of success.

There is one matter which I hope will be included in the list of subjects to be discussed in the course of these conversations; I refer to trade relations between Canada and the United States, particularly in the light of certain actions taken at Washington, the unhappy effect of which has been to restrict the importation into the United States of Canadian agricultural products.

There have been in the course of the past year and a half two palpable breaches on the part of the United States of the general agreement on tariffs and trade which in each case have directly affected the importation into the United States of the agricultural products of Canada and other countries.

The United States entered into the Geneva agreements by executive action under authority of congressional legislation. The extensions of the agreements as a result of the subsequent conferences at Annecy and Torquay were also carried into effect on behalf of the United States by executive action under authority of legislation passed by congress. But, Mr. Speaker, in the year 1951 the United States congress took a step which had the effect of violating not only the spirit but indeed the terms of the general agreements on tariff and trade. I refer to section 104 of the defence production act of 1951. An amendment, known as the Andresen amendment, was tacked on to the defence production act with a view to excluding from the United States market Cheddar cheese, butter and other dairy products.

The then president of the United States, Mr. Truman, expressed his strong disapproval of that amendment but in the end he felt himself unable to veto the amendment on account of the fact that the remainder of the defence production act was urgently needed legislation which he felt obliged to support and to put into effect by presidential signature. That amendment, as I have said, not only violated the spirit but it directly violated the letter of the general agreements on tariff and trade; because under those agreements it was provided that there should be on the part of signatory nations no action taken to raise barriers against trade in commodities which I have mentioned.

However, that is not the end of the story. The Canadian farmer did feel the effect of that Andresen amendment, and as of January 1, 1953, further Canadian agricultural products were affected by action in Washington. As of that date quotas were imposed on dried whole milk, dried buttermilk, and dried cream, which will have the further effect of restricting exports of those Canadian agricultural products to the United States. As is well known, that action affects of course the export of similar products to the United States from other countries which are parties to the general agreements on tariff and trade. Very strong protests have been lodged and indeed, in some cases, threats of retaliatory action have been heard from Australia, New Zealand, Denmark and the Netherlands.

The matter apparently does not end there, Mr. Speaker, because we hear reports from Washington at the present time that in congress additional steps are being debated to impose further restrictions on the import of Canadian agricultural products into the United States. This time it applies to grains, and while it is to be hoped that the debate on that matter will not result in restriction of importation into the United States of Canadian grain products, nevertheless it could become a very serious matter for the Canadian farmer. Lest hon. members should think that the export of Canadian grain to the United States market is not a serious matter, may I remind the house of some figures which were placed on the record by the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) on May 1, 1953, which are to be found at page 4652 of Hansard. They indicate that in the year 1952 our exports of grain to the United States were as follows:
Exports of those grains to the United States for the first two months of 1953 showed

a very substantial reduction; but the figures for the full year of 1952 are sufficient, I think, to indicate that when congress debates proposals to impose restrictions on the importation of Canadian grain into the United States it is a serious matter indeed for the Canadian farmer.

Some of these restrictions take the form of quotas, Mr. Speaker, and I think in that respect recognition should be given to the fact that quotas can be a much more effective barrier to trade than some of the more conventional tariffs imposed in other days. A distinguished Canadian businessman, Mr. Rhys Sale, president of the Ford Motor Company of Canada, in a speech in January, summed the matter up in these words:

Tariffs are of much less significance today than the multiplicity of import controls imposed by many countries,"" Mr. Sale declared, and added that these restrictions ""often throttle trade much more effectively than any tariff.""

Recognition must be given, I think, Mr. Speaker, to the danger that is involved in this action on the part of the United States in 1951 and again in 1953-with further restrictions now under debate. The matter is raised at a time when a good deal of concern is being expressed in this country for the future of the general agreement on tariffs and trade.

In the debate which we had in this house ten days ago on the subject of trade, when discussing the estimates of the Department of Trade and Commerce, I recall that there was general agreement expressed in all parts of the house in favour of the extension of the general agreements. It must cause a feeling of very serious disquiet, Mr. Speaker, when we anticipate expiry of these agreements at the end of the calendar year, to see that departures from them not only have been taken in Washington but apparently there are further departures under debate in the United States congress. The feeling in this country should be brought to the attention of the authorities in the United States in a most vigorous way.

We have had made available to us in the last several days the figures of trade for the first three months of this calendar year. May I read some paragraphs from the dominion bureau of statistics daily bulletin of April 28, 1953:

Total exports-domestic and foreign-in March were valued at $313,000,000, down nearly 13 per cent from the value of $359,300,000 for March, 1952. Aggregate value for the three months ending March was $913,900,000 as against $1,001,800,000, a decrease of 8-8 per cent. In contrast, the value of imports In the month rose over 10 per cent to an estimated $360,400,000 compared with $327,000,000 last year, raising the three-month aggregate almost 9 per cent to $998,200,000 as against $916,100,000.
U.S. Trade Restrictions

Based on the estimate for imports, Canada thus had an import surplus of $47,400,000 in trade with all countries in March and of $84,300,000 in the three months. These figures compared with an export surplus of $32,300,000 in March and $85,700,000 in the quarter last year.

Commodity exports to the United States were up in value in March to $206,400,000 from $188,700,000 a year ago, bringing the total for the quarter to $575,000,000 against $551,700,000. Estimated value of imports, however, showed a greater rise to $274,300,000 for the month from $253,500,000 and to $764,700,000 in the three months from $694,000,000 last year. The import balance with the United States rose moderately in the month to $67,900,000 as against $64,700,000 and for the three months climbed to $189,700,000, in comparison with $142,300,000 for the first 1952 quarter.

Total exports to the United Kingdom in March were down sharply to $38,800,000 from $69,000,000 a year earlier, accounting for most of a decline in the three-month value to $124,600,000 from $157,400,000 last year. On the other hand, imports rose in value to an estimated $37,600,000 in the month from $22,600,000, and in the three months to $95,300,000 from $68,200,000.
The result was an export surplus of only $1,200,000 in March as against $46,300,000 last year, and of $29,300,000 for the quarter as compared to $89,200,000.
Total exports to other commonwealth countries and to other foreign countries, and also imports from these countries, were down in value from last year both in the month and three months.

Mr. Speaker, while we may take some comfort from the fact that exports to the United States in this three-month period increased as compared with the three-month period of last year, the house will have noticed that our imports during the three months rose very substantially as compared with the same three-month period for 1952, and that our import balance in those same three months in 1953 shows a substantial increase over the same three-month period in 1952. All this must be considered against the background in which our exports to all countries are showing a decline. Let us hope this will impress upon the Canadian government the necessity for doing everything in its power to reduce this import balance with the United States by increasing the export of our Canadian agricultural surpluses to the United States.

I think that we, as a House of Commons, should tell the government that we expect the government to take the most vigorous action possible, in the light of these direct and deliberate breaches on the general agreement on tariffs and trade by Washington. At a time when the western nations carrying the banner of freedom in a world struggle, whether it be on hot fronts or cold fronts, are pinning their standard to the principle of good faith in international agreements, then I say there never was a time when it was more important that the nations of the world which have entered into an agreement such as the general agreement on tariffs and

U.S. Trade Restrictions trade, and particularly the United States as a world leader in trade, should adhere with the most scrupulous respect to the agreements into which they have legally and voluntarily entered. This general agreement on tariffs and trade was entered into with the full sanction of law at Washington.

Nothing less than the most vigorous action, the most vigorous presentation of the claims of Canada in this respect, will do justice to the Canadian farmer and the legitimate grievances that he and all Canadian citizens have in the face of the deliberate breach by Washington of the general agreement on tariffs and trade. It is timely therefore, I think, that the Prime Minister should be going to the United States to discuss with the president matters of common concern.

In the hope of giving to this subject a place of high importance on the list of subjects being discussed at that conference, and in the hope that the House of Commons will express itself in a manner that will indicate to the parties at Washington that Canada does take a very serious view of the action of congress in violating the letter and the spirit of the general agreement on tariffs and trade, and underlining the importance of this matter of the export of Canadian agricultural products to the United States, I should like to move, seconded by the hon. member for Kamloops (Mr. Fulton), the following amendment:
That all the words after ""that"" to the end of the question be deleted and the following substituted therefor:

in view of the impending departure of the Prime Minister for Washington this house desires to record its opinion that further and more vigorous efforts should be made by the government to bring about the removal of the restrictions imposed by the United States on the importation of Canadian agricultural products, in violation of the general agreement on tariffs and trade.

May I have the indulgence of the house for a moment to mention two figures which I have worked out, with some strain on my mathematics. The figures for the first three months of this year concerning our trade with the United States show that the United States took 63 per cent of the total Canadian exports, and that our imports from the United States compose 77 per cent of our total imports. These figures show a substantial rise in the proportion of our imports which we took from the United States in this three-month period of 1953 as compared with 1952.

This matter has been discussed in the house on a number of occasions this session, although no motion has been moved similar to the one now before the house, and therefore we shall support the amendment. I want to say, however, that
IMr. Fleming.]

we endorse the suggestion made by the hon. member for Eglinton (Mr. Fleming) that every step possible should be taken, and every representation possible made, to see if some alteration may not be made in United States policy regarding trade, and particularly the importation of farm commodities into that country.

I think we have all been alarmed not a little by the reports that have come to us from Washington. It is true that when President Eisenhower took office most of us thought that what he had to say indicated he was in favour of a liberalization of trade and commerce. However, his recent appointment to the tariff commission of the United States of a gentleman who is known to be a high protectionist fills some of us with misgivings. Then, the requests for further powers to control import of farm produce being made by Mr. Benson, the secretary of agriculture, still further emphasize the misgivings that we have. Recently suggestions have been made that the profitable market we have enjoyed for coarse grains over the border from western Canada may be denied to us at least in part. That would be a serious thing for western agriculture.

It was remarked in the house the other night-by the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner)-that there is something that we have become so used to that we have overlooked it, namely that already there are substantial barriers against the importation of Canadian wheat into the United States. It is true that under the GATT agreement the duty-and I am speaking from memory- was reduced from 40 cents to 20 cents a bushel, or cut in half in any event; and that was looked upon as a concession to us. But in the regulations dealing with flour, the milling of wheat and so on in the United States, provision is made that domestic grain must constitute the major part of any flour milled there. Those are protectionist measures that affect our agriculture, apart altogether from the recent violations of the Geneva agreement on tariffs and trade that our government put into effect-without the authorization of parliament but in good faith -when they interfered with the importation of cheese and other dairy products into the United States.

I think it is time that this house and this country spoke in no uncertain terms. We owe the United States nothing as far as aid to this country is concerned. We have paid our own way. We are in a different position from that of almost any other country trading with them in the world. Most countries are beholden to the United States for substantial aid. We are not. I think

we can speak out clearly. The figures given in the last sentence by my friend the hon. member for Eglinton (Mr. Fleming) are, I believe, within one per cent, the same figures I put on the record in connection with the debate on trade and commerce a short time ago.

I want to say that when the Prime Minister goes to Washington, no matter how strongly he makes our representations-and I know he will make them courteously-I feel confident that he will have behind him in those representations the entire membership of this house.

1734404,ca.proc.d.1953-05-06.21.3,1953-05-06,ba7c8691-5f1c-4bc4-9ec1-82c0a828db16,ca.m.1501,Mr. Victor Quelch (Acadia):,,UNITED STATES RESTRICTIONS,,,1 just wish to say a few words in support of the motion, Mr. Speaker. I think we have every reason to be extremely critical of the attitude of the United States with regard to placing further prohibitions against the importation of goods from this country. After all, the United States were the promoters of the idea of non-discrimination in the Geneva trade agreement. They were the ones who were so insistent upon that principle being included in the Geneva trade agreement. That fact made it almost impossible for the nations of the sterling area to balance their payments.

Consequently, escape clauses were put in the agreement and the nations of the sterling area were allowed to place restrictions against imports. They were obliged to do that on account of the fact that they lacked dollars. Therefore they had to place restrictions against imports from the dollar area and to try to expand their imports from the sterling area.

But that is not an excuse that the United States can make. The United States have not an unfavourable balance of trade. On the contrary, they have an extremely favourable balance of trade. Therefore, if the United States want to continue to export on a heavy scale, they must be prepared to accept imports from the other nations or, on the other hand, be prepared to make large-scale foreign investments in those countries that need their goods, or make gifts in a manner similar perhaps to that of the Marshall plan.

I am therefore hoping that when the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) meets the President of the United States he will stress this point strongly, pointing out the need for making it possible for the nations in the sterling area to buy goods from the dollar area either by a policy of foreign investment or of gifts to those nations.

I believe that the United States embargoes on agricultural products and the trend in the United States toward greater restrictions and more protection are extremely serious for Canadian agriculture and for our whole Canadian economy.

I cannot allow this moment to pass without saying that we in this group over the years, ever since I have been a member of it, have been warning this government that this is exactly what would happen, namely that as soon as we lost the British market and came to depend upon the United States market we were depending upon a market that was competitive in many respects, that was uncertain, and that was liable to future restrictions. I cannot for the life of me understand the United States breaking a serious agreement with democratic nations such as the agreement on tariffs and trade. How they can hope to promote co-operation in economic matters, when they set such a terrible example as they have set in recent months, is something I cannot understand. I think Canada is justified in talking to the United States in the strongest possible terms.

I do not profess to be an economist, but in the study I have made of economics one point is emphasized time and time again, namely that if the world ever again faced a major depression it would be because of the economic policies of the United States. If these restrictions on imports affected only the United States, we would not have to worry about the matter. But United States economic policies affect the whole world. I think Canada would be justified in taking the strongest possible measures to see that some improvements are brought about.

Our market in Britain-and I have said this time and time again-for cheese, bacon and eggs is gone. We are depending now more and more on the United States market. I totalled up the quantity of Canadian grain which the United States purchased from Canada last year. It amounts to $160 million. That is an increase of over $100 million in our exports in those products to the United States since 1949. We are glad to see that increase, but I think that fact demonstrates how important it is to Canada that further restrictions by the United States should not be placed against our agricultural products. Our economy in Canada today is relatively prosperous in most industries with the exception of agriculture. 1734406,ca.proc.d.1953-05-06.21.5,1953-05-06,dcd2258a-b8c3-4099-bffb-7b24cce8341e,ca.m.9761,Right Hon. L. S. St. Laurent (Prime Minister):,Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council,UNITED STATES RESTRICTIONS,,,Mr. Speaker, it is of course possible, on the motion for the Speaker to leave the chair for the house to go into committee of supply, for resolutions expressing opinions of the house to be adopted without there being necessarily a vote of no confidence, because the rule is that when that kind of motion is accepted and disposed of, the motion that the Speaker leave the chair can be immediately renewed and dealt with again. I take it that this was not intended to be a motion of no confidence; it was intended to be an expression of the feeling of all members of parliament that further vigorous efforts should be made by the government to bring about a removal of these restrictions which are causing serious concern and even embarrassment. Of course when we discuss matters of this kind some of us go farther than others. I do not want to be taken as admitting that we have lost the British market. Circumstances have developed which have made it difficult, if not impossible, for the British consumers, because of their balance of payments situation, to take from us all they would like to get from us. I would not like to admit that we have been moving towards dependence on the United States market. We are anxious to be world traders and we are glad to find opportunities to trade wherever these opportunities may be developed.

It would be quite helpful if a unanimous expression of opinion were registered in this house before I have these interviews that I am looking forward to with the President, the Secretary of State and perhaps other members of the administration, and I hope some members of the United States senate and congress. I would hope that those discussions could be carried on in the friendly
spirit in which all our mutual problems have been discussed over many years now.

Perhaps the hon. member who has moved this would not mind striking out of the third line these two words ""and more"". It might have implications both as to the tone and as to the kind of measures or efforts that have been made up to the present time; it might have implications that I would prefer not to have to put forward unless circumstances became such that it was obvious that friendly efforts to bring about a more acceptable situation were doomed to fail. So, I suggest it should read:

In view of the impending departure of the Prime Minister for Washington this house desires to record its opinion that further vigorous efforts should be made by the government to bring about the removal of the restrictions imposed by the United States on the importation of Canadian agricultural products, in violation of the general agreement on tariffs and trade.

I hope the hon. gentleman who has moved the amendment will be prepared to suggest that these two words ""and more"" might be dropped and the house would consent to their being dropped. The motion could then be regarded as an expression of the unanimous opinion of all hon. members. I would feel more comfortable in exhibiting the message to have it without these two words, and to have it as an expression of the unanimous opinion of the Canadian House of Commons.

1734416,ca.proc.d.1953-05-06.21.15,1953-05-06,103e48f0-b6bb-43eb-9c06-7ceffaf3ea78,ca.m.7989,Mr. Stanley Knowles (Winnipeg North Centre):,Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation,UNITED STATES RESTRICTIONS,,,Mr. Speaker, I have just a few words to say. First of all I wish to join with others in welcoming most heartily not only the introduction of this amendment but also the readiness of the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) to accept it, with the slight change he has suggested.

I am sure the house deeply appreciates the Prime Minister's attitude. I gather he regards the passing of this amendment in its altered form as what it was intended to be, namely the strengthening of his hands in connection with his trip to Washington for the balance of this week. I am sure we all appreciate the tremendous importance of the economic policies of the United States, not only as they affect our own economy in Canada but as they affect the economic well-being of the entire world. And the Prime Minister carries with him the best wishes of the House of Commons and of Canadians generally, in his mission to Washington.

The other reason I felt it was appropriate for me to rise at this time was to suggest that this day must be regarded as a red-letter day in our parliamentary history, and must be placed alongside June 12, 1951, and August 27, 1946.

This will make three occasions in the last seven years when amendments to motions to go into supply have been carried by the house without involving want of confidence in the government, or defeat of the government of the day. As the Prime Minister knows, we have made frequent references to those two other occasions, particularly when the argument has been put forward by the government or its supporters that they could not vote for some amendment moved by the opposition because it involved a want of confidence in the government.
U.S. Trade Restrictions

The action taken today is similar to that taken on June 12, 1951, when an amendment asking for a committee on procedure was before the house, and similar also to the action on August 27, 1946, when we were discussing the question of a milk subsidy. It becomes clear that if the government agrees with and is prepared to consider a proposal put forward by the opposition by way of an amendment to the motion to go into supply, it need not involve want of confidence in the government. In other words amendments of this nature are opposed by the government only when the government is opposed to their substance.
As some hon. members may have observed,

I have already indexed this incident in my own little black book for -use on future occasions. As I say, we now have three instances in the last seven years when the house will have passed amendments to motions to go into supply. This is an exceptionally appropriate occasion for that procedure, and I would hope that in the future when other similarly worth-while proposals are offered to the house in the form of amendments to go into committee of supply we will not be confronted repeatedly with the argument that they are motions of no confidence and that therefore they cannot be accepted.

Let us have more of this facing up to issues on their merits. The proposal made today by the hon. member for Eglinton (Mr. Fleming) has been recognized as one that is good, on its merits, and because of that the government has agreed to it. I hope there will be more of this when other amendments are moved in the future. Meantime we are pleased the amendment is to be accepted. I thought, however, that this statement should be put on the record in light of the fact that, along with the other occasions I have mentioned, this is another red-letter day in parliamentary procedure.

1734422,ca.proc.d.1953-05-06.22.1,1953-05-06,0daa460f-b2c1-447e-abbe-c4bd1f237b32,ca.m.6630,Mr. H. R. Argue (Assiniboia):,,REQUEST FOR ANNOUNCEMENT OF INITIAL PAYMENT,,,I rise at this time to ask that the initial price for wheat be established immediately. Not only is it necessary, as far as the farmers are concerned, to have a firm price announced at this time now that seeding operations are becoming general; I feel that the government owes it to this house to say what that initial price will be.

We in the C.C.F. group believe that any suggestion that the initial price that prevailed last year will be satisfactory again this year is not correct. We believe that the selling price under the international wheat agreement, together with the increase in the floor price, is sufficient to justify a substantial increase this year in the initial price for wheat. The ceiling under the international wheat agreement has been increased from $1.80 per bushel to $2.05 per bushel; the floor price has been increased from $1.20 per bushel to $1.55 per bushel; and even if one subtracts the 6 cents per bushel handling charge that will no longer be paid after July 31 there remains a substantial increase in both floor and ceiling prices.

With the deduction of the 6 cents per bushel the ceiling price is increased by 19 cents per bushel, and with the deduction of the 6 cents per bushel the floor price is increased by 29 cents per bushel. The Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) said that he expects that even though Great Britain has stayed outside the wheat agreement they would still buy substantial quantities of wheat from Canada. In every statement that the minister has made to parliament during this session in regard to wheat prices he has said that prices will be higher this year, that the wheat board will receive a higher return for wheat.
That being the case, I think the $1.40 per bushel that was paid as an initial price last year is too low and that the initial price should be increased by 25 cents per bushel

to $1.65 per bushel. The announcement of such an initial price should be made immediately. As I say, the farmers are now on the land in western Canada carrying on their seeding operations. They are deciding at this time what acreage they will sow to bread wheat, to durum wheat, to oats and to barley. The Minister of Trade and Commerce has announced the initial price for oats; he has announced the initial price for barley; but he has not announced the initial price for wheat.

He has said that it will not be lower than last year, but he left the actual initial price that will be paid up in the air. That is a different stand from that taken by the government in connection with this matter in the last three years since the conclusion of the United Kingdom wheat agreement. In 1950 the initial price for wheat was announced on April 5; in 1951 the initial price on wheat was announced on May 4; last year, 1952, the initial price for wheat was announced on April 8. In other words, in those last three years the government announced the initial price before seeding became general, at a time which would give an opportunity to the farmer to plan his production on the basis of the initial prices that had been established.

But for some reason the announcement is being delayed this year. The Minister of Trade and Commerce says that he is going to wait until the end of July when all the factors can be taken into account. If he can wait until July, he could wait until August or any other time and all the factors of supply and demand will not be known even then because they vary and change from time to time.

We had an experience in western Canada with wheat prices in 1949 which I do not want to see repeated. Just a few weeks before the election in 1949 a final payment of 20 cents per bushel was made. The farmer went to the post office and received a cheque for 20 cents per bushel on wheat which had been sold perhaps three years before. Next week there was another cheque for 20 cents per bushel, and following that still another one for 20 cents per bushel. They were all jammed in just before the election date. In addition the expectation was held out that there was going to be another substantial final payment.

It served a good political purpose but I do not think it did the wheat board system of marketing grain any service. It may have increased the number of votes for the Liberal party at that time, but it probably decreased the votes by twice as many when the farmers finally discovered that the last payment available for the five-year pool was only
Wheat-Initial Payment 3 * 8 cents per bushel before the additional $65 million was paid.

I say that now is the time to announce the initial payment for wheat for this year, not a floor initial payment that can be jockeyed around late in July just two or three weeks before August 10, a probable election date. There should be an announcement now that the initial price will be increased in view of the increase in the ceiling price under the international wheat agreement. The increase in the initial price should be a substantial amount. I think that that suggestion is perfectly justified.

It used to be said and it can still be said that one of the advantages in making an initial payment, an interim payment and a final payment was that the farmer had his income spread throughout the year. That is not nearly as important now because farmers are unable to market all their grain in the fall. Farmers have to spread out their income from grain receipts because of the quota system. It used to be that a farmer could market all or nearly all of his grain in the fall; but when the interim payment came just before seeding it was very helpful and highly acceptable to the farmer. The final payment probably came about Christmas time. The experience we have had this year is that we had an initial quota of five bushels per acre-so that is all the income we could get early in the fall. Then that quota was gradually increased and the income from selling the wheat has been spread out quite evenly because the small quotas were gradually increased.

I am one in this house who is very optimistic about crop prospects this year from information I have received through conversations and in mail which I am getting from western farmers. The recent rainfall and snowfalls in March, April and early May have provided a substantial moisture reserve. If we get a reasonable amount of rainfall in June and July we could get another very large crop of grain. If we do get another large crop of grain, in addition to the carryover farmers will have on their own farms, then we are certain to have only a small quota when the harvest begins.

It is not only farmers who need increased income by way of an increase in the initial price, but our merchants in western Canada, who throughout the summer months advance money to farmers on the basis of the crop that is going to be harvested, need to get their accounts paid as quickly as possible. I suggest that an increase of 25 cents per bushel in the initial price, bringing it from $1.40 to $1.65 a bushel on the basis of No. 1 northern in store at Fort William, is fully

Wheat-Initial Payment justified as far as the farmers are concerned. The wheat board's income is sufficient to justify initial payments in that amount and to allow for further additional payments. A higher initial price is needed to increase the farmers' income in the fall when he must pay his accounts with local merchants.

We would not be nearly as interested in this particular aspect of wheat marketing if the government had made some provision for loans for grain stored on the farm in suitable farm storage. If that had been done farmers would have had a means of obtaining the income they need. We have asked for that provision but the government has said no. Today we are asking, first, that the announcement of the initial price for wheat for this year be made firm, and second that it be increased by a substantial amount. I do not think that the initial price for wheat should be left up in the air until the end of July. From what we heard yesterday, that is likely to be only two or three weeks before the general election.
Because I feel that this is a necessary provision, and that it is a reasonable provision, I propose to move the following amendment, seconded by the hon. member for Melfort (Mr. Wright):
That all the words after the word ""that1' to the end of the question be struck out and the following words be substituted therefor:

this house is of the opinion that consideration should be given to an increase of 25 cents in the initial payment for No. 1 Northern wheat basis in store Fort William/Port Arthur or Vancouver for the crop year beginning August 1, 1953, so that the said initial payment will be $1.65 per bushel.""
I hope this motion will commend itself to the government in the same way as the motion adopted this morning.

,Co-operative Commonwealth Federation (C.C.F.),,Hazen Robert Argue,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=0daa460f-b2c1-447e-abbe-c4bd1f237b32&Language=E&Section=ALL

1734425,ca.proc.d.1953-05-06.22.4,1953-05-06,546df72b-fbe3-4980-ad0f-abc7a4ceed2a,ca.m.876,Mr. D. S. Harkness (Calgary East):,,REQUEST FOR ANNOUNCEMENT OF INITIAL PAYMENT,,,I should like to support the representations made by the hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Argue)

Certainly I think that an increase is justified on the basis that the maximum and minimum prices under the new international wheat agreement have been increased by approximately that much. 1734426,ca.proc.d.1953-05-06.22.5,1953-05-06,fdce9d46-5c36-4ca6-b6c7-52d1e6f9ba0b,ca.m.8192,Mr. Solon E. Low (Peace River):,,REQUEST FOR ANNOUNCEMENT OF INITIAL PAYMENT,,,I think

perhaps I should say just a word about the amendment that has been moved by the hon. member for Assiniboia. I followed carefully the statement he made in support of this amendment, and the arguments that he used.

At the moment I am looking at the amendment entirely from the point of view of the people of my own constituency, Peace River. I think the people in that area would ask for an increase in the initial payment partly on the ground that their quota, even though it may be set at a fairly high rate during a certain year, is not able to be filled because

there is not enough storage space in the whole Peace river country to allow them to deliver their wheat. As a consequence, most of our farmers up there have to hold their wheat over for quite a long period of time.

We know from experience that the Peace river country is about the last from which grain is taken for filling our commitments overseas. As a consequence, when there is a shortage of cars or when the terminals are filled with grain, these people are forced to hold their grain much longer than they are in other places in the dominion. They are the last to be considered. As a consequence, a higher initial payment would be of great benefit to them. I am supporting the amendment on that basis alone.

I do not know just how the people in other areas would look upon it. I suppose that in some sections of the wheat growing area they would say: Well, if we get a higher initial payment it may force the wheat board to borrow more money and if they borrow more money they will have to pay more interest; then, if they pay more interest that money will come out of the returns to us. It would not be, therefore, a matter of tremendous concern to some of them, especially in areas where they have a good quota and shipments are taken out very rapidly to fill our export commitments. I cannot speak for those people.

Speaking entirely from the point of view of the people in the Peace river country, I feel that it would be very helpful if the initial payment were raised somewhat. What that figure is I would not be prepared to say. The amendment calls for 25 cents a bushel, and I think that would be reasonable and my people would want me to support the request made by the hon. member for Assini-boia (Mr. Argue). 1734427,ca.proc.d.1953-05-06.22.6,1953-05-06,1716566b-edef-40b2-9552-49510618c3bb,ca.m.9539,Right Hon. C. D. Howe (Minister of Trade and Commerce):,Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce,REQUEST FOR ANNOUNCEMENT OF INITIAL PAYMENT,,,I think perhaps, Mr. Speaker, I should distinguish this amendment from the one that was adopted before the luncheon hour. This amendment is definitely a motion of lack of confidence, and must be treated as such. As I understand it, the hon. member complains that I did not make a specific announcement of the initial price for wheat when I spoke in the debate on ratification of the wheat agreement. I think that I was as definite at that time as the circumstances would allow. It is taken for granted that we have a renewal of the wheat agreement for the next year; that is not strictly true. All the countries except Britain have voted in favour of an agreement, but to date no country has ratified the agreement. Canada expects to do so within the next

Wheat-*Initial Payment week or two. I am sure the other countries will move in that direction, but it must be kept in mind that certain parliaments are not in session and it may be difficult to get all the ratifications within the time limit that is required to make the agreement operative.

Fifty per cent of all the participants, including the United Kingdom, need to ratify the agreement before July 15 in order to make the agreement operative. I think, in announcing a price that will be no worse than $1.40 as an initial price, and may be a larger amount, the government was going about as far as it could under present circumstances. It accepted the advice of the wheat board, as it is bound to do under the wheat board act, and made the reservation that if after July 15 the situation warranted a higher price a higher price would be announced. I think the farmers of western Canada who have had experience over the years in pooling wheat are not wedded to an unduly high initial price. I think most of them recall the serious difficulties that the pools encountered in earlier days through announcing too high an initial price.

We have set up a pattern to which we have been able to adhere, that is an initial price of $1.40 and an interim payment in the month of March before seeding, then a final payment after completion of the final accounting for the crop year. I believe that pattern has commended itself to our producers. I am sure that a substantial payment in the month of March is just as valuable as would be higher payments in the months of September and October when wheat is being delivered. I question very much whether the mover of this motion has the support of any large segment of western producers in asking for a substantially higher initial price. However, that is my opinion as against his.

The hon. member has been advocating storage on the farm for a long time, and he has advocated it again today. May I point out to him that the opportunities for storage on the farm will never be so richly rewarded again as they are at the present moment. If anyone cares to carry his wheat over into the next year and deliver it after the first of August, I am quite sure he will be well rewarded when the receipts for the next crop year are distributed. At the moment, I think he cannot complain very much about lack of payment for storage on the farm.

Wheat-Initial Payment reward anyone who cares to hold over his wheat. It will be interesting to see what class of farmer takes advantage of this opportunity to profit by storing wheat on the farm.

I might point out that the government does not set the initial price. It approves the initial payment, but the initial payment is recommended by the wheat board, and properly so. It is recommended by the board after the board has assessed the possibilities of selling the crop. It is a payment which the board can assure the government is a proper payment to be made. Hon. members know that in undertaking the marketing of crops of western Canada, the government did not undertake to proceed on other than a business basis. I am sure hon. members would not expect the government to set initial prices that it believes could involve a loss. I am rather surprised, after the statements my hon. friend made in his early remarks about the huge surpluses of wheat in the world, that he would now feel justified in saying that the government should enlarge the initial payment. If the situation is as bad as he represented it to be, and if there is to be no wheat agreement, possibly the present initial payment of $1.40 will be found to be fairly satisfactory before the year is over.

1734437,ca.proc.d.1953-05-06.22.17,1953-05-06,3f8478c9-237c-49c9-b8d2-585121332655,ca.m.6252,Mr. Stuart (Charlotte):,,REQUEST FOR ANNOUNCEMENT OF INITIAL PAYMENT,,,Before this item

carries I should like to say a few words in connection with a visit I made to the United Nations during March. I shall describe my experience at New York as briefly as possible, but I do feel it my duty to say just a few words in this connection.

My first comment would be a few words of well-deserved praise or credit to those who so well represent this country at the United Nations. The contributions made by our Secretary of State for External Affairs and by our Minister of National Health and Welfare are very well known the world over. These gentlemen are held in the highest esteem by all democratic countries represented at the United Nations. I believe I should also include David M. Johnson and the staff who are with him in New York. I believe they would all be placed in that same category.
Previous to my visit at the United Nations I had been led to believe that those representing this country at the United Nations and

Supply-External Affairs at other international assemblies had been chosen perhaps for a very soft assignment where a good time was enjoyed by all with very little work or responsibility. I want to say that after my short experience there I most certainly have changed my views. I wish to congratulate those efficient representatives and indeed the entire staff who are with the Canadian delegation at the United Nations. Those outstanding civil servants are working very long hours.

For example, the first meeting would be called at nine o'clock in the morning; and at no time did we have to wait for a quorum. They were all ready to go to work at that hour. Then, at ten o'clock they moved away to the sessions of the United Nations, which were carried on from eleven o'clock until one o'clock in the afternoon. Then there was the afternoon session, which would last until nearly six o'clock. Then at night the delegates would get together and more or less prepare their agenda for the next day.

I well remember one evening while I was there a complaint being made by one member of the delegation because he was not able to get a stenographer at eleven o'clock at night. Those are the hours that the civil servants with this delegation are obliged to work. I must say they are most efficient and most courteous to all members of the delegation, and I believe they are doing a most creditable job and one which should be appreciated by all Canadians.

Before resuming my seat I wish to say a few words in connection with the United Nations-and in what I have to say I shall be very brief. On many occasions we read criticisms of the United Nations. It is true that many of the things we had hoped they might be able to accomplish have not been accomplished. I believe however that they deserve a great deal of credit for what they have already done.
Let me list just a few of those accomplishments:
The United Nations effected peace between Israel and the neighbouring Arab states.
They stopped armed hostilities between India and Pakistan over Kashmir.
Through their efforts warfare was stopped and a free and independent United States of Indonesia was established.
They were also responsible for the withdrawal of British and French troops from Syria and Lebanon in 1946.
In the same year soviet forces also withdrew from northern Iran.
On the recommendation of the general assembly the former Italian colony of Libya became an independent nation.
Supply-External Affairs
In the Balkans they were responsible for a much improved condition on the northern borders of Greece.
In Korea they have taken history's first collective action against aggression.
The United Nations have also universally adopted a declaration of human rights, the first international proclamation of the fundamental rights of human beings.
Through its various agencies the United Nations have fed nearly ten million children.

I believe this wonderful organization is doing a wonderful job. When one sits in the United Nations and looks around, seeing the representatives of 60 different countries, realizing that 55 of those 60 are of one mind, and that they are fighting for world peace, it gives him a grand feeling of security. I believe it is the only thing we have today upon which we can depend, so far as our hopes for world peace are concerned. We should cherish it, and do everything in our power to support it in every way.

,Liberal,,Andrew Wesley Stuart,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=3f8478c9-237c-49c9-b8d2-585121332655&Language=E&Section=ALL
1734438,ca.proc.d.1953-05-06.22.18,1953-05-06,c10e3486-b954-4a50-b28f-1e4e6b0b944d,ca.m.8869,Mr. Stewart (Winnipeg North):,,REQUEST FOR ANNOUNCEMENT OF INITIAL PAYMENT,,,Mr. Chairman, I should like to make one or two comments following what was said by the hon. member for Charlotte. No one questions the correctness of what he has said about the hard-working ' members of our permanent staff. I had the opportunity and the good fortune to be at the UN last fall for about five weeks, and I realize that five weeks does not give anyone the right to speak with authority on the subject. I do not pretend to do so at this time. However, I have one or two suggestions to make, and I trust they will not be construed as criticisms. Far from it; they are suggestions which have crossed my mind, and which I now offer tentatively to the minister.

In the first place I did feel that many of the key members of the staff were overworked. I have been told that if our delegation at the UN were to be properly manned it would almost denude the east block. I do not know whether that is so or not. But I do know that when an individual has to make a decision, the consequences of which may be far-reaching, he is not best able to do so when he is tired and fatigued. I have seen members of our permanent staff frequently in that state.

If one is going to think with crystal clarity, such as at times is demanded in connection with certain problems discussed at New York, one has to be fresh, to be physically fit. to do so. The decisions arrived at may be important.
Then I have another suggestion to make to the minister. Again, this is not by way

of criticism of members of parliament who go to the UN, especially members on the government side of the house who serve as chairmen representing Canada on particular committees. My own experience, as an observer, was that I learned very much more by going where I wanted to go and when I wanted to go, rather than being tied down to one particular seat or committee. In view of the fact that whoever represents Canada by occupying a seat at a committee is going to say what government policy is to be, would it not be a better idea, particularly from the point of view of members of the Commons and of the Senate, if a permanent civil servant were to occupy the chair and members of parliament were to act in an advisory capacity behind him, freeing themselves at the same time to go on occasion to other committees and thus acquire a greater grasp of what is taking place?

As the hon. member for Charlotte pointed out, the delegation holds morning meetings. Sometimes I have wondered if those meetings were not in the nature of a re-hash of what happened the day before, when the person occupying the chair in each committee would give a brief analysis of what had taken place on the previous day. After all, one could get all that information from the pages of a daily newspaper. I am wondering if it would not be more profitable if the delegates were to discuss important problems which were likely to come up in the near future.

These are only suggestions which I put forward tentatively, and without any intention whatsoever of criticizing. I offer them, without knowing too much of the ins and outs of what goes on. However, what I have suggested may have some value.
