1734456,ca.proc.d.1953-05-06.22.36,1953-05-06,85a45525-d20a-41db-8c2a-1b91c360656b,ca.m.7972,Mr. Coldwell:,,REQUEST FOR ANNOUNCEMENT OF INITIAL PAYMENT,,,"Mr. Chairman, I have some remarks to make on this item and I may be longer than I might otherwise have been at this stage of the session.

During the past few weeks we have discussed the necessity for national defence and how best to co-operate in that field with those who are determined to prevent aggression. We spent some time considering Canada's domestic and external trade, and again how best to protect and expand it for the improvement of living standards in Canada and the world. Yesterday we discussed some recent statements which have
been made by the Soviet union and by President Eisenhower concerning international matters.

Now we turn to the external affairs estimates which have been thoroughly discussed by the standing committee and recommended to the house for adoption. I wish to emphasize one point today in connection with our external activities which in my opinion ultimately will be our best form of defence against communist, fascist, or indeed any other form of aggression against our democratic way of life.

In our domestic relationships we must continue to provide and include social services, including a national health plan, but we live in a world where we cannot hope to maintain high standards ourselves unless we assist in the rapid development of the underprivileged and underfed in the rest of the world as well as in our own land. That was the purpose of our adherence to the Colombo plan. Under it we agreed to appropriate $25 million for a commonwealth scheme to assist certain of our fellow citizens in southeast Asia. Our appropriation this year of $25,400,000-$400,000 to be used in our country to assist students and technicians to learn something of our resources, our social services, and so on-is organized in the interests of our own people as well as of others.

The Colombo plan is the most imaginative of plans approved and adopted by the commonwealth countries and we are very glad to support it wholeheartedly. However, the annual report of the Department of External Affairs for 1952, at page 29, states that the Colombo plan is designed to supplement assistance being given to south and southeast Asia under the United Nations program. It is also designed to implement capital development schemes being undertaken under that plan by increasing supplies of trained men and women in southeast Asia. It points out that the Colombo plan differs from the United Nations program because assistance is arranged on a purely bilateral basis by agreement with the governments co-operating. It is organized entirely apart from the United Nations; the co-ordination of the program and the general supervision of its operations being exercised toy the council for technical cooperation in Colombo, which is made up of representatives of participating governments assisted by a small bureau.

Canada's part in the Colombo plan, I want to say, has been well worth while and, under an able administrator in the person of Mr. Cavell, is doing excellent work; but the Colombo plan was originally designed to supplement assistance in the areas of south and

southeast Asia under the United Nations program. Indeed, and I want to impress this upon the minister and the house, we believe that as soon as possible it should be more closely integrated with the United Nations plan for technical assistance for underdeveloped countries.

In a speech which the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Pearson) made in November, 1952, he made this quite clear. Indeed he said that technical assistance for underdeveloped countries was the one firm and clearly defined basis upon which to build mutual understanding ""between east and west"". The minister noted that there were two programs of technical assistance to which the Canadian government adhered and which many Canadians were actively participating in, and then went on to say, and I quote him:
The first and more important of these is the United Nations expanded technical assistance program.

He then went on to outline what is being done under the United Nations plan and noted that in addition to the $25 million, which parliament approved as a contribution to the Colombo plan for economic development, the government had also asked parliament-as it does again this year-for an appropriation of $400,000 to the commonwealth technical cooperation program for south and southeast Asia. In this speech the minister emphasized that the Canadian government regards the Colombo program for technical co-operation as a temporary supplement to the technical assistance activities of the United Nations and specialized agencies in south and southeast Asia. He said that it was important to ensure that every effort is directed towards integrating them to as large an extent as possible. Then he went on to express the hope that the United Nations, if it is given appropriate support for its activities in this field, will be able to assume in three or four years the major responsibility for technical assistance in southeast Asia. He tells us that Canada is urging the greatest possible use of all United Nations agencies offering technical assistance to south and southeast Asia. That, I believe, should be the aim which the minister and the government and all of us should keep in mind.

However-and now I am going to make a few criticisms-Canada's part in discussions at the United Nations, in connection with the expanded technical assistance program and the specialized agencies, does not, I think, begin to fulfil what we expect of our part in it or what our people believe we are actually doing. Indeed, none of the United Nations countries seem willing-not only Canada; none of them seem willing-to provide the necessary financial assistance to carry out

Supply-External Affairs what must be a comprehensive and worldwide plan. In the first period from July 1950, to December, 1951, 56 nations, including one of the recipients, India, contributed together just over $20 million. Canada's contribution was $850,000 in Canadian currency.

In the second period, which comprised the whole of 1952, less than $19 million was subscribed by 65 nations, but only just over $17 million was actually collected. This time Canada subscribed $750,000 or $100,000 less than would have been the case had the total contribution for that year exceeded $20 million.

In 1953, the third period, the economic and social council recommended that a minimum of $25 million should be provided. Actually, subscriptions have amounted to just over $21 million. Canada this year promised to contribute $750,000 and obligated herself to subscribe an additional $100,000 if the total should reach $25 million. This total was not reached but I have already stated in the figure I have given that the amount exceeded $20 million and, subsequently, Canada agreed to pay $50,000 more or $800,000 because the total pledge had exceeded $20 million-and our present estimate is for $850,000 in Canadian funds.
Now, if we look at Canada's record we find that in the first period of 18 months Canada gave an unconditional $850,000. In

column2: however, we gave $750,000 with the promise of an additional $100,000 if the total reached $20 million. We thus made a portion of our contribution conditional, but in

in spite of the fact that the target was $25 million, Canada promised exactly the same $750,000 plus the same $100,000 if the total reached not $20 million as in the previous year, but $25 million for this year.

column1: Thus the government's actual enthusiasm for this most significant of all the United Nations plans lessened each year in spite of the eulogistic speeches made by the Secretary of State for External Affairs, the Prime Minister and indeed other members of the government at the United Nations and in various parts of Canada. Each year the Canadian position became worse rather than better. Surely this is not a record of which this parliament can be proud, particularly as we boast of having the largest per capita trade in the world and standing third among all the nations in the volume of world trade.

I want to say something in connection with these contributions. There is something here which appears to be about as small as one can possibly conceive. I want to say at once that I cannot imagine that it was done at the direction of the Secretary of State for External Affairs, the Minister of Finance or
Supply-External Affairs indeed the government. I think perhaps it was done by a zealous official who was trying to save a little money on the exchange.

In 1951 and 1952, when our dollar was at a discount, our contributions were stated to be payable in Canadian dollars. Last summer, however, our Canadian dollar was above par and still is, so that this year we have pledged ourselves to contribute the equivalent of 750,000 United States dollars. In other words, in the eyes of the world we shall appear to have been mean enough to try to save for Canada a relatively small amount of $10,000 or $15,000, at 2 per cent, by way of exchange at the expense of the technical assistance organization of the United Nations. As I say, I do not think the Secretary of State for External Affairs was responsible for that. I do not believe the government is, and I doubt very much whether any member of the government is aware of it.

column2: rather expect that an opportunity to save Canada $10,000 or $15,000 was seized by an overzealous official. The estimate of $850,000 now before us is in Canadian dollars. Surely the attempt at such a saving places Canada in a very false and unfavourable light when this is realized by other contributing countries. When we consider that no real attempt has been made to put into full effect article
of the NATO agreement, which calls for economic integration among the participating countries, we have little to be proud of in the field of economic aid to the United Nations program.

column1: Now, Canada participated in the discussion in the economic and social council, and I understand we actually supported the recommendation that the budget for technical aid for 1953 be increased from the just over $17 million collected in 1952 to the target of $25 million for 1953. In other words Canada recommended a general target increase of approximately 31 per cent, but has finally agreed, according to the estimate now before us, to increase our own contribution by only 13 per cent, less a 2 per cent difference in exchange, making it 11 per cent.

This is no example for a comparatively rich country to set to countries that have less financial ability and fewer resources. It may be said that during the first period only about one-third of the money collected was actually spent; that is true. The rest, however, was carried forward and therefore gave the technical aid organization additional money in the second period. Failure to expend all the money, of course, was due to the fact that the organization was not fully equipped to do the job effectively, and governments which were expected to take advantage

of technical aid were not alive to the possibilities of the program. This was indicated very clearly during the second period, 1952, when approximately $17 million was collected and nearly $23 million was spent. The program of the United Nations in this field has now got under way and the underdeveloped nations are beginning to ask for the kind of assistance the organization should be prepared to extend.

I was at the United Nations recently, but only of course for a week end. While there I went into some of these matters, and I learned that this year, 1953, requests from the underdeveloped countries are literally pouring in. I was told that there are at least twice as many requests already as it will be possible to meet with the funds available. By the end of the year, without any encouragement from the technical aid agency, there will probably be four or five requests for every one that can be met.

At the general assembly, at which I was present in 1950, it was emphasized that the operations of the technical aid agency would be of an expanding character. It was said that as the programs proved their value and as countries increased their requests for additional aid, additional funds would naturally be provided. The considerations, as I remember, outlined at the assembly, were primarily proof that the countries wanted assistance, and that the specialized agencies were capable of providing it.

Now, after almost three years, a study of the operations of the technical aid agency shows clearly that both these conditions have been fully met. But just at the time when the countries which need the aid have become vitally interested, and just when the agencies have been established to'do the job, adequate funds are not being provided by the nations -I am not saying by Canada, but by all the nations. Additional funds promised as the agencies expand are not forthcoming, but are remaining, as the figures indicate, practically static. Let me repeat that Canada joined in the recommendation for an increase in the amount to be budgeted by 31 per cent, but under the estimate now before us is promising an additional 13 per cent.

If we believe, and I think we do, that technical assistance is as important as we say it is, we should demonstrate the fact by contributing more than the cost of hauling the soil to fix up the land around the new bureau of statistics building on Tunney's Pasture, and other buildings in this city. I am subject to correction on that. When it is put that way, we begin to realize how pitifully
MAY e, 1953
small our own contribution is, and why we have very little to boast about in connection with this plan.

Again I am going to say that we may have something to boast about in connection with the Colombo plan, though we should do more. But we contribute $800,000 to the United Nations technical aid, and we spend as much annually or more in hauling soil to cover Tunney's Pasture and to landscape grounds around some of our buildings. Indeed, all the nations together are proposing to spend on this important plan only $25 million. This was regarded as being a very important plan. If the target were reached, $25 million a year is certainly not significant enough to justify all the fine talk that Canada and other countries indulge in about the importance of this activity. If we think that our countries really believe technical assistance is important, we should demonstrate it by being willing to contribute altogether more than the cost of a single destroyer for each year's activity.

Now, the minister may say that we are giving $25,400,000 a year to the Colombo plan. This, however, is being used for technical and financial assistance in a few but admittedly quite important areas in southeast Asia. Contrast this, however, with only three-quarters of a million or thereabouts which we are willing to pledge for the United Nations agency for work which we voted to begin, which we voted to expand, and for which we promised additional funds as the expansion proceeded. Not only the minister of external affairs but the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) and others, have several times indicated that the real hope for the future peace of the world is in the field of assistance to the underdeveloped areas.

I believe, and when I say this I speak for those associated with me, that we are not going to defeat communist aggression, communist propaganda, by force of arms. The only way in which we can defeat the propaganda and that aggression is by the extent to which we are able to increase the standards of living of the underprivileged, underdeveloped people in the world. As long as from one-half to two-thirds of the human race go to bed hungry every night, they are not going to listen to all our theories and talk about democracy. To them a handful of rice, a bowl of gruel is far more important than the right to speak freely or to vote or to do any of those things. It seems to me this is the crux of our defence against communism. Wherever it has shown its head, wherever it has gained its control, it has
Supply-External Affairs been where there was poverty, misery and want.

I should like to say that I am quite sure the Canadian people agree with that point of view. In support of this opinion I should like to quote just one resolution by a public body and another by a legislature in Canada, which indicate the support of Canadians for the technical assistance program. The one I am about to quote was passed on January 17 at the annual convention of the Canadian Federation of Agriculture. This is how it reads:
Whereas we believe that the best hope for ultimate world peace lies in an expansion of the program of technical assistance to underdeveloped countries now under way by the United Nations;
And whereas Canada's annual contribution to this program amounts to only $850,000 or less compared with Norway's contribution of more than $3,000,000;
And whereas Canada is contributing $25,000,000 a year for six years to the Colombo plan;
And whereas Canada's combined contribution to these two programs amounts to approximately one per cent of the annual defence appropriations;
And whereas we believe the technical assistance program of the United Nations is in need of a substantially greater sum than its annual budget of $25,000,000;

Therefore be it resolved that this annual meeting of the Canadian Federation of Agriculture strongly urge the government of Canada to appropriate substantially greater annual amounts for the technical assistance program of the United Nations.

May I say that since that resolution was passed I have had letters from at least one farm organization and others from farm people in western Canada who have urged that, in addition to this, we should do something to supply actual food requirements even as gifts to some of the needy nations of the world. Usually Pakistan and India are mentioned in the correspondence that I have received. As far as Norway is concerned, may I also say that in addition to that national gift-and this is a highly interesting piece of news-there is an all-out drive to further boost that effort by a plan called ""From People to People"" where the ordinary people-a population of 3-2 million-are asked to contribute further sums for aid to the underprivileged, by giving at least one day's pay or income. His Majesty King Haakon in launching the program said this:

Let us start this program in the firm conviction that the thing we are doing is the only road that leads to a happier world, better international understanding, and the fulfilment of humanity's great prayer: freedom from want.
Surely what Norway is doing we, with our resources, can do as well.
I also want to emphasize the statement- which I believe is correct-that Canada's contribution both to the Colombo plan and

Supply-External Affairs the United Nations technical agency amounts to 1 per cent of the defence appropriation which we have already adopted in the estimates now before us. I say that this does not, I am sure, convey an accurate picture of the desire of the Canadian people.

With regard to the resolution passed in a legislative assembly, the following resolution was moved by W. J. Berezowsky, M.L.A., in Regina on Thursday, April 2, 1953. It is rather long and I may not put all of it on the record, but I will put on the relevant parts. May I say that this resolution was passed unanimously. Both the C.C.F. members on the government side and the Liberals on the opposition side voted in favour of it. The resolution was as follows:
This assembly, recognizing the critical situation that endangers the peace of the world and the need for governments to assess and reaffirm their position in regard to international affairs,-

column2: affirms its full support of the principles of the United Nations which, despite its shortcomings, remains an essential agency for building world peace;

reaffirms its belief that mankind's hope for lasting peace can be realized only through a comprehensive and spectacular program of economic and social advance in every part of the world, since military preparedness, deemed necessary by U.N. in the present international situation, cannot take the place of positive action to end poverty and exploitation;
urges the federal government to press for world economic progress and world peace by:

column1: Then there are a number of clauses which I will read.

column2: allocating available raw materials in accordance with need;
planning the development of world resources to the highest possible degree;
providing technical and capital assistance to underdeveloped areas on a scale many times greater than the amount now available for these purposes;
taking international action to achieve maximum production of food and providing for its equitable distribution;
establishing international development corporations for these various purposes, which would be free from control by private capitalism or by any one country;
increasing the scope and resources of the Colombo plan;
planning an expansion of world trade based on consideration of world needs;
achieving greater equality, on a high level, of living standards everywhere;

column1: Perhaps I should put the other four clauses on the record as well, although they do not deal with the same matter:

column2: resisting attempts by any nation to use the U.N. for selfish ends;
supporting the inclusion of all nations who will support the charter of the U.N.;
insisting that any action against aggression undertaken by the U.N. be completely under the control of the U.N.;
working towards the abolition of the veto in the United Nations.

column1: As I say, that resolution was passed unanimously on Thursday, April 9, 1953.

What I have done just now is place on the record a resolution from the federation of agriculture, representing an independent farm group in the country and the resolution passed in one of our legislatures dealing quite largely, although not entirely, with the matter under discussion.

As the committee knows, ever since the United Nations was set up, I have been interested in these matters. I had the great privilege of representing Canada for a great deal of the time on the committee which set up the economic and social council of the United Nations. I take little credit for what Canada did at that time because, after all, the able advisers who were assisting-although I might have spoken the words-were the people who really were responsible for much that I proposed at that time.

I should like to join with others and pay tribute to our staff in the Department of External Affairs-and in the Bank of Canada, incidentally, in this instance-because we have an extremely able group of people there. I have been interested in these matters; and because I was absent from the committee and from the house owing to illness when these questions were under consideration by the standing committee on external affairs, I wished to say something about them even if I have perhaps trespassed on the time of the committee when hon. members and the minister are extremely busy indeed.

,Co-operative Commonwealth Federation (C.C.F.),,Major James William Coldwell,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=85a45525-d20a-41db-8c2a-1b91c360656b&Language=E&Section=ALL
1734457,ca.proc.d.1953-05-06.22.37,1953-05-06,103e48f0-b6bb-43eb-9c06-7ceffaf3ea78,ca.m.7989,Mr. Knowles:,Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation,REQUEST FOR ANNOUNCEMENT OF INITIAL PAYMENT,,,Mr. Chairman, I am sure it is not necessary for me to emphasize the fact that we have just listened to one of the most important speeches to have been made in this session of parliament. I am satisfied that nothing is more basic to the future peace of the world than that we take far more seriously than we have done to date this question of our responsibility to try to assist the underdeveloped portions of the world to get on their own feet and to raise their standards of living to something comparable to what thus far has been achieved in the west.

I shall not take the time of the committee to repeat what has been so well put by my leader, the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar. However, I should like to say something about one aspect of this attempt to provide technical assistance under various United Nations programs and also under the Colombo plan. I refer to the question of bringing young men and young women from these underdeveloped areas to Canada in order to educate and instruct them so they might be able to go back and play a significant part in helping to develop their own countries.

This is just one aspect of the broad program of technical assistance concerning which my leader has sought to challenge the thinking of the committee this afternoon, but it seems to me that it is an exceedingly important aspect of the problem. Indeed, the chances of underdeveloped areas getting on their own feet and to the point where they can produce sufficient food so that hundreds of millions of people need not go to bed hungry every night depends upon our transmitting to a large number of people in those areas the advantage of the education and the training that we have here in the west.

As my leader has pointed out, the number of human beings who go to bed hungry every night of their lives is staggering. We know that in countries like India, one of the members of the commonwealth to which we belong, there are millions of people who enjoy only one meal a day throughout their lives. We cannot solve that problem adequately only by sending food, much as we should do along that line. But it is our responsibility because it is the right thing to do, and it is the crux of our own defence, to try and play our part in helping to educate these people so they can do the job themselves. If we could provide an imaginative educational program I believe we would see a change in the living standards of a country such as India and other areas in south and southeast Asia within the space of a generation. But, Mr. Chairman, what have we done with respect to this educational part of the technical assistance program?

I am going to give the committee a few figures. I will not bother in each instance to say which page of Hansard they will come from but I shall give four different references in Hansard now and hon. members will know that the figures I shall give shortly are to be found on those various pages. The Hansard references are March 9, 1953, at page 2730; March 18, 1953, at page 3051; and February 26, 1953 at page 2415. One of these references, namely the first one I gave, involves a cross-reference to Hansard of March 28, 1946, at page 357. On these pages will be found order paper questions of mine and the answers given by various departments, and in the case of the reference to 1946 an order paper question of the hon. member for Quebec South and the answers that were given to him on that occasion.

As one looks at the information contained on these various pages he will find that today under the technical assistance program of the United Nations, under the Colombo plan and under other plans of that sort, we have brought to Canada, for training here, students from foreign countries to the number of only 243. Ninety-nine of these are under
Supply-External Affairs the Colombo plan; 123 under United Nations programs; 16 under UNESCO, 3 under FAO and 2 under ICAO, adding up to 243.

Canada has spent all told, including the supplying of facilities for these 243 people whom we have brought to Canada for this purpose, $338,748.88 which can be earmarked as such; but it would appear that to be fair there should be added to that another figure of about the same size which would bring it up to something of the order of $750,000. But, Mr. Chairman, that is the total figure. That is all we have done under this technical assistance program. All credit to those who have got this program going and have done this much, but by comparison just look at what we have done under some other programs which we appear to have taken much more seriously.

For example, under NATO we have entered into certain agreements to bring people to Canada for military training. The number we have brought under these agreements to date is 3,063, and we have spent on their training $140,734,857.92. In other words, we have these two programs going along more or less concurrently, training under NATO agreements and training under United Nations technical assistance and similar programs, but we have spent out of Canadian funds 190 times as much on the training of foreign military personnel under NATO as we have spent on the training of foreign students under various forms of technical assistance.

If one were to go back, still looking at the Hansard references I have already given, to the tremendous job that Canada did under the British commonwealth air training plan during the war, he would find that under that plan we trained in Canada from other countries of the commonwealth 68,174 persons, and Canada spent on their training, apart from what was spent by other countries, $1,589,954,609.94. In that instance we spent more than 2,000 times as much as we have spent all told on the education and training of young people from other countries under technical assistance programs.

I suggest, Mr. Chairman, that these figures as to what we did under the British commonwealth air training plan and what we have done and are doing under NATO indicate what can be done when there is the determination to put the program over. Real accomplishments were made or are being made under those programs, and Canada has credit coming to her for that, but here apparently the old maxim applies: ""where there's a will there's a way."" There was a will to do something under these programs, and it was done.
Supply-External Affairs

It would look to me, Mr. Chairman, as though we have not yet faced up to the challenge of this other task of helping to train people from these underdeveloped countries so they might be able to go back and do a job in helping to raise the living standards of their own countries in a way that could be done by improving their methods of agricultural production and by expediting their industrialization. I urge most strongly that the remarks of my leader today be given very serious consideration not only by the government but by members of the house in all parties and by Canadians generally, and that we put some real drive into these very important programs.

We hear this slogan used a good many times these days: ""Trade, not aid"". I was interested in what the Secretary of State for External Affairs had to say about that yesterday. It seems to me that though the slogan in a very good one, and certainly very plausible, the fact of the matter is that aid may be necessary for a long time, and I hope that the valid emphasis which is being put upon trade will not result in our thinking that something is being done about trade when it is not, and that therefore we may lessen our aid. It seems to me that aid is going to have to take the form of food and the material supplies that are necessary. It is going to have to take the form of machinery and goods to assist these people in other areas, and I suggest also that a very important contribution that Canada could make would be to increase tremendously the bringing of students from these other countries right here to Canada for the type of training that would really benefit these other lands.

It is a disgrace that the amounts we have spent on this important work are so small. I believe it is up to the government, it is up to all of us in the house, all of us who are in public life, to try to give, if that is what is needed, leadership to our own people, to encourage support for programs of this kind. We should do it because, as has already been pointed out, it is the crux of our defence. We should do it because it is good in itself; it is the right thing to do to try to help the peoples of other areas of the world to rise at least to the living standards that we enjoy in our own country.

column1: 1734478,ca.proc.d.1953-05-06.23.2.14,1953-05-06,3f27b0a5-3b86-4f3a-8bab-f44a940c0742,ca.m.9024,Mr. Adamson:,,LABOUR CONDITIONS,DEPARTMENT OF EXTERNAL AFFAIRS,,"Mr. Chairman, this item deals with the international joint commission which, in turn, deals with the St. Lawrence deep waterway. In view of the fact that the Secretary of State for External Affairs and the Prime Minister are both going to Washington tomorrow, I think something should be said in the house on this matter before they leave.

This morning we had what amounted to a protest against the attitude of the United States with regard to trade. I wish now to make a protest with regard to the attitude of the United States concerning the St. Lawrence deep waterway. But before I do so I wish to speak very briefly about the suggestion that two canals can be built. That is fallacious, because the situation on the St. Lawrence is completely different from the situation at the Soo. At the Soo there is a narrow isthmus between two great lakes. One side of that isthmus is wholly in Canadian territory and the other side is wholly in United States territory. Therefore parallel locks or parallel canals could be built running wholly in United States territory and wholly in Canadian territory.

On the St. Lawrence that is not so; because on the south bank it is partly in United States territory, being in the state of New York, and it is partly in Canadian territory in the province of Quebec. And, I may say, I would be very much surprised if anyone would start off to build a canal where the premier of Quebec knows no other Caesar. In the United States, if the canal were built from the Quebec boundary to lake Ontario it would be a perfectly useless structure, because it would lead from the blank wall of the boundary of Quebec and the international boundary in Canada to lake Ontario. In other words we would be duplicating half a canal, and building a whole canal on the other side. Therefore that suggestion in my view is ridiculous.

Coming now to the action of the United States, I wish briefly to chronicle what has happened in the last quarter century in this regard. In 1926 there was a report of a subcommittee of the senate to the committee on foreign relations, dealing with the great lakes-St. Lawrence basin. They went back virtually to the original report produced in the time of the Coolidge administration and submitted to President Hoover. In 1926 these
Supply-External Affairs were the findings of that committee, and I think for the purpose of my protest I should place them on record:
The conclusions of this commission are therefore:
First. The construction of the shipway from the Great Lakes to the sea is imperative both for the relief and for the future development of a vast area in the interior of the continent.
Second. The shipway should be constructed on the St. Lawrence route, provided suitable agreement can be made for its joint undertaking with the Dominion of Canada.
Third. That the development of the power resources of the St. Lawrence should be undertaken by appropriate agencies.

Fourth. That negotiations should be entered into with Canada in an endeavour to arrive at agreement upon all these subjects. In such negotiations the United States should recognize the proper relations of New York to the power development in the international section.

That was the 1926 report to the president by the body set up under the United States senate, and favouring in four specific instances and for four specific reasons the construction of this St. Lawrence seaway, and the construction of the hydroelectric power development. The United States senate committee had this to say in its report in 1946, referring to the earlier committee:
The overwhelming majority of the Senate foreign relations committee reported that the Senate advise and consent to ratification of the treaty.

That was in the days when we were endeavouring to have the St. Lawrence deep waterway constructed by means of a treaty. There you have a committee advocating in the strongest possible terms that an immediate start should be made on the St. Lawrence deep waterway and hydroelectric power development. That was 27 years ago, over a quarter of a century, and the economy of the North American continent has been bedevilled by selfish interests which have been able, because of the peculiar set-up of the United States constitution, to set at nought the wishes of the sovereign United States government. Not only that, they have been able to subvert completely and destroy the wishes and desires of three Canadian governments as expressed in this house.

There comes a time when the patience of a people becomes exhausted, and I suggest that that time has arrived. The United States senate committee report of 1946 made reference to the groups which were opposed to this, and I think the following words are significant because they reinforce the protest I am making at the present time:

Many groups have claimed that the seaway will be injurious to their vested interests. Among these are the railroads, port cities, coal interests, and lake carriers. The claimed disadvantages spring primarily from the age-old tradition of preferring the status quo. It is noteworthy that every technical and mechanical advance in the history of the world has been viewed by some with

alarm. This was true of the railroad, the automobile, the aeroplane-of the development of each new resource and each section of this country. But the nation has become great by utilizing every natural and human resource at our command.
There is reason to believe that the main opposition to the seaway comes from the eastern railroads.

I emphasize again that that is the report of a United States senate committee, made in 1946. Before I refer to the findings of that committee I should like to deal briefly with the question of power development. We are now in the fifth month of 1953, and have virtually lost all chance of construction during the summer season. The province of Ontario will probably be facing a power shortage in two years or possibly less. The industrial growth of this country will be penalized even if construction were to start immediately. Every month, every day, every hour this project is delayed costs the economy of Canada large sums of money. That is the result of the actions of selfish interests elsewhere.

At that time the senate committee-I mention this merely because I have heard the argument-went into the question of the possibility of developing power by atomic energy. Perhaps I should quote just one or two sentences in their findings, because there is a growing feeling that atomic energy will replace all other forms of energy in the production of power. They said:

The concern expressed by the opposition that atomic energy for commercial purposes would be likely, in the foreseeable future, to render hydroelectric energy obsolete was minimized and answered by the proponents. The crux of the proponents' case was that, according to the best current estimates of the experts on atomic energy, the cost of producing this new energy cannot very well be less than that of fuel-burning steam plants, and it is likely to be much higher. Since St. Lawrence power costs less than the cost of producing power at steam plants with fuel costs disregarded, there does not seem to be much reason to fear that atomic energy would be cheaper than St. Lawrence power.
A number of quotations from authoritative sources relating to atomic energy were introduced into the record.
They mentioned the General Electric Company and many others whose representatives gave testimony in that regard.

I come now to the report of this committee, which found in favour of the development of the St. Lawrence deep waterway. It found that the estimated saving in the cost of transportation would be as high as 50 per cent in the case of joint rail and water rates and much higher in the case of all-rail rates. I should like to bring to the attention of the minister their final statement, which was as follows:
The committee has also considered the question of the navigation rights of the United States in the

wholly Canadian sections of the great lakes-St. Lawrence system in the light of fears expressed by the opposition that present treaties do not vest in the United States adequate rights in these waters. The committee has concluded that these fears are totally unwarranted in view of the express terms of the treaties on this point.
That is true because the 1909 boundary waters treaty specifically granted equal rights to the United States and Canada in boundary waters and in canals on the great lakes.

What can be done about this? We have waited 27 years, and apparently we are very little nearer to our goal. Because of the constitution of the republic known as the United States of America the opposition are able to thwart the wishes of a huge majority of the people of the United States. They thwart not only the unanimous wishes of the United States but those of their best friend and best customer.

We are given highest hopes; we are given publicity in newspapers, but we are not given any concrete evidence that the attitude of those interests who can, and probably will, thwart the desire of our joint countries has changed. I can give one example of this, and I wish to quote Mr. R. J. Ireland, president of the D. B. Hanna Company, which is interested of course in coal but also in the Labrador iron development. He said, regarding the St. Lawrence deep waterway that- -people . . . are unanimous in the opinion that the St. Lawrence waterway project would be a detriment and not a help to us; so I can tell you, sir-
And those are his words to the committee.
[DOT]-in so far as the Labrador project is concerned, my company is much more interested in it as an investment for the future, without a seaway, than with a seaway-

The D. B. Hanna Company is interested in the development of the Labrador iron deposits. At the time this statement was made the company was interested in the Mesabi iron range as one of the greatest ore-carrying fleets on the great lakes, as well as one of the greatest individual coal producers in the United States.

What did Mr. Ireland mean by that statement some years ago? If he meant anything, he meant that as far as he was concerned the Labrador iron deposits were going to be held dormant. No other interpretation can be taken from that statement. What has changed that opinion is simply that the Mesabi iron range is running out. The supply of high grade iron ore in the continental United States is rapidly being exhausted, and the D. B. Hanna Company as well as many others will have to look elsewhere for their supplies of iron ore. They have had a change of
Supply-External Affairs conscience, and they are all for the St. Lawrence deep waterway.

Mr. Chairman, I mention that to show the sort of thing we are up against, the sort of interests we are up against in this St. Lawrence deep waterway. There has been the ability to rally just enough members of congress and members of the senate to defeat this thing every time it has come up. Twenty-seven long years have we waited. Twenty-seven long years have we put up with procrastinations, with ""wait a little more"", and ""give us a little more time"" and ""let us see a little more about this"".

,Progressive Conservative,,Agar Rodney Adamson,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=3f27b0a5-3b86-4f3a-8bab-f44a940c0742&Language=E&Section=ALL

1734481,ca.proc.d.1953-05-06.23.2.17,1953-05-06,3f27b0a5-3b86-4f3a-8bab-f44a940c0742,ca.m.9024,Mr. Adamson:,,LABOUR CONDITIONS,DEPARTMENT OF EXTERNAL AFFAIRS,,Mr. Chairman, how long are we going to wait? I tell you that the situation requires action, and it requires action in this way. I think there must be a deadline stated, that we must be prepared to state it now, after which deadline we shall give notice-as we are quite entitled to do-that the 1909 treaty shall be terminated within a year. After that treaty has terminated the rights of United States ships in our canals, on an equal footing with our own, are also terminated. We then can impose on United States traffic such discriminatory tariffs, such embargoes, and such other methods as will make them see what they are paying for the strange attitude they have followed.

I believe, Mr. Chairman, that the time has come when we cannot longer leave this to promises of good will. We have seen every president since Coolidge thwarted in his desire to go ahead with this development. We have seen every national convention of both major parties in the republic to the south include the development of the St. Lawrence waterway as a fundamental plank in their program. We have seen, irrespective of whether there were Republican or Democrat governments in the United States, that there were interests which were powerful enough to thwart the desires of the people. I do not believe that we in Canada can put up with this sort of thing any longer. I think we should say so in the possible hope that somebody will see the danger.

Today the general belief in Washington and New York is that Canada is bluffing. I assure you, Mr. Chairman, that we are not bluffing. The canal can be built without the hydroelectric development. It can be built without in any way encroaching on the sovereign soil of the United States. It would be fantastically expensive from an engineering or an economic standpoint to build the canal without the hydroelectric power development;

Supply-External Affairs it would be ridiculous, but all the same it could be done. A canal could be built around the international rapids, without touching the international rapids. A canal could be built wholly and completely in Canada by Canadians with Canadian capital and machines. We would be loath to do such an uneconomic thing, but if we are going to be kicked about and if the sovereign desires of this parliament and this country are going to be thwarted by interests which are inimical to the welfare of this country, then we may have to consider that line of action.

The minister is going to Washington and the Prime Minister is going to Washington, and I know they will receive the welcome from the United States government and the President of the United States that all our prime ministers and secretaries of state always do. It should be pointed out that it is not the government of the United States which is at fault. They are doing everything they can to assist in the mutual development. The statements of the secretary of state of the United States about international trade could not have been fairer or freer. But it is that strange minority who are apparently able, because of the constitutional type of government enjoyed-perhaps ""enjoyed"" is not the right word, but that is what it is-by the United States, to throw a monkey wrench into the desires of both our countries which causes our patience to be damn near exhausted.

1734484,ca.proc.d.1953-05-06.23.2.20,1953-05-06,51c861ef-0f17-4a79-8d9b-0854fb3ef33f,ca.m.6889,Mr. Pearson:,Secretary of State for External Affairs,LABOUR CONDITIONS,DEPARTMENT OF EXTERNAL AFFAIRS,,I was going to say just a word about technical assistance under the other item, but perhaps I can do so under this item. In view of the remarks that have been made by hon. gentlemen opposite, I should like to say something.

I am not going to boast about the record of the government in the field of technical assistance, because it does not warrant boasting. I am not going to apologize for it, because it does not deserve apology. The government appreciates the importance of technical assistance to underdeveloped countries. Some years ago we expressed the feeling that, when practicable, that kind of work should be done through the United Nations. Since I made that statement we have had a great deal of experience with the operation of the Colombo plan, the item which we are now discussing. I feel that operation has been very successful in its technique, and

that leads one to wonder whether or not- other things being equal-from the practical point of view more results might not be achieved more quickly by bilateral arrangements between the country making the contribution and the country receiving the contribution.

Nations?

,Co-operative Commonwealth Federation (C.C.F.),,Major James William Coldwell,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=85a45525-d20a-41db-8c2a-1b91c360656b&Language=E&Section=ALL
1734486,ca.proc.d.1953-05-06.23.2.22,1953-05-06,51c861ef-0f17-4a79-8d9b-0854fb3ef33f,ca.m.6889,Mr. Pearson:,Secretary of State for External Affairs,LABOUR CONDITIONS,DEPARTMENT OF EXTERNAL AFFAIRS,,However, the United Nations certainly has a legitimate interest in this matter, and we support that interest. Whatever might be the best way of doing it, certainly there should be no overlapping with the United Nations work. One of the encouraging developments in recent years has been that the tendency to overlapping and duplication of two or three years ago has been reversed.

There is, I think, very effective co-ordination among the various agencies in this field. There are a good many such agencies. There is the United Nations technical assistance program. There is the Colombo plan, the item which is under discussion. There is the Point Four program of the United States, and there is the work being done by the international bank in the field of capital assistance. There is the work being done by FAO and other United Nations agencies. At the present time the economic and social council is discussing the setting up of another agency, the international development fund. It is, therefore, more important now than ever before that this co-ordination should be achieved. There should be a minimum of duplication.

So far as Canada's record in the United Nations is concerned we have subscribed, as has been pointed out by hon. gentlemen opposite, a fairly high percentage of the total amount raised by the United Nations. The only countries whose contributions to the United Nations schemes have exceeded those of Canada in amount have been the United States, the United Kingdom and France. Our contributions have been quite close to those of the last two countries. In relation to other countries, proportionately, our record is not bad. It may well be that the United Nations should have agreed to try to raise more than the amounts that have been agreed upon. On that point I will only say that the experience of the first year or so with the United Nations technical assistance program underlined the difficulties of spending effectively and practically the amount raised. But these difficulties, as the hon. gentleman pointed out, have been now substantially removed.
The Colombo plan, I think, is operating very effectively, and will be operating more
effectively as we get more experience. We are asking parliament this year to contribute $25 million, plus an amount of $400,000 for technical assistance itself.

There have been some general statements made in the discussion of these earlier items on the importance of technical assistance to underdeveloped countries, and I would agree with everything that has been said. I would certainly accept the viewpoint that starvation and misery are the breeding grounds of communism. But the corollary is not always true. We should not forget that a high standard of living does not, itself, necessarily mean peace. Before 1941 the Asian country which had by far the highest standard of living was Japan. But Japan brought more misery, destruction and suffering to Asia during those years after 1941 than any of the other countries of that continent. While starvation and misery should be fought and should be conquered if possible, because if we do not succeed in that battle communism may succeed, that victory will not of itself necessarily make for peace.

I should like to mention one other point before I sit down. Nearly every speaker on the other side who spoke on this subject made a comparison between what was called the ""niggardly amounts"" that we spend on assistance of this kind and the amounts we spend on national defence. This comparison is dramatic but, without further analysis and explanation, it could be rather misleading. I believe it is right for us to assume that the first obligation of the government and parliament of the country is to prepare for the defence of the country. If that is not done successfully, if with our friends we cannot through adequate preparation deter aggression, and if we then do have aggression because of our weakness, technical assistance will not be of much help. Recognition of this primary obligation of national defence is given by the very countries who are so much in need of help and technical assistance.

Some Asian countries who are being helped, who need and deserve our help, are spending themselves a very high proportion, perhaps as high as 50 per cent, of their national revenues on national defence, and not always defence against communist aggression. I believe that is one factor that might be mentioned.

The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre pointed out how few students we have received from Asia under this scheme. He gave the figures and they were not, of course, very impressive. He talked about 300 or 400 times as much money being devoted to NATO military exchanges as to

Supply-External Affairs Colombo civilian exchanges. You could also, if you wish, make the rejoinder here that the very countries that need that kind of technical education so much also find it necessary to spend 200 or 300 times as much on military preparations in building barracks and things of that sort as they spend on building technical colleges. It is, therefore, a complicated problem. I do not think we necessarily clarify it by making the kind of comparison that is so often made between the amount now spent on defence and the amount spent on this kind of assistance.

I wholeheartedly agree with what the President of the United States said in that inspiring statement he made a week or two ago. If we could cut down our defence expenditures-and we must look forward to the day when we can do that-then any money that can be saved in that way could surely be devoted to schemes of assistance under the United Nations and under bilateral arrangements. If that can be brought about, the very fact that we are cutting down on our defence expenditures will be an indication that some of the tension, some of the fear and some of the anxiety in the world will have been removed. This will be conducive to profitable and constructive work in this field, and in that work I feel quite confident that Canada will play, as I think she is playing now, a worthy and useful part.

1734497,ca.proc.d.1953-05-06.23.2.32.2,1953-05-06,1716566b-edef-40b2-9552-49510618c3bb,ca.m.9539,Right Hon. C. D. Howe (Minister of Defence Production):,Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce,LABOUR CONDITIONS,DEPARTMENT OF EXTERNAL AFFAIRS,DEPARTMENT OF DEFENCE PRODUCTION,"Mr. Chairman, for a number of reasons it is not my intention to make a lengthy statement at this time, as a good deal of information relating to defence production has been placed before the house in recent months.

Copies of the annual report of the Department of Defence Production for the calendar year 1952 have recently been made available to all hon. members. This report outlines changes that have taken place in the raw materials situation, and the progress that has been achieved in the defence production program. In addition, it indicates the effects that the changes in emphasis within the defence program have had on the organization of the department. At the end of the year,
[The Chairman.]

the progress we had made in decontrolling materials was reviewed by my parliamentary assistant in this house. Any further developments since that time have been publicly announced. One program that has properly attracted the attention of many hon. members is the CF-100 and Orenda engine projects at A. V. Roe. However, I made a detailed statement on this subject in the house as recently as February 16.

Another source of information on the defence picture has been the parliamentary committee on defence expenditure, which has met regularly since January 27, 1953. Finally, my department has answered 188 parliamentary questions which, when broken down into their subquestions, total 880 inquiries. For these reasons, I do not feel that the house would wish a lengthy statement from me at this time, and I shall confine my remarks to a few general comments.

We have now completed two years of our defence program, and it might be useful to consider the place of this program in our economy now and what it is likely to be in the next few years. Let us turn first to the materials side. Hon. members will recall that following the outbreak of hostilities in Korea a serious world-wide shortage of strategic raw materials developed as a consequence of the needs of accelerated defence preparations, as well as of scare-buying by the public at large. This shortage naturally caused a general increase in prices. Through the close co-operation of government and industry, increases in the prices of a number of strategic materials produced in this country were held to a level consistent with rising costs. This accomplishment made an important contribution toward the stabilization of world prices and therefore to the whole allied cause.

It was obvious, however, that in certain lines increased production was required above everything else and, in order to achieve this, some incentive price increases were permitted. In some instances additional capital cost allowances were granted in order to supplement normal incentives already provided by the special tax concessions available to various industries.

This policy of stimulating production of essential materials has been remarkably effective. Canadian output of petroleum, base chemicals, non-ferrous metals, iron ore and steel in the last two years has expanded significantly. Hon. members will be familiar with many of the major programs now under way which will still further add to the productive capacity of the country.

Today the free world is no longer suffering from the acute general shortage of strategic materials that existed 18 months ago. Indeed, of the dozen or more materials previously allocated by the international materials conference, only nickel and molybdenum are still under controlled allotment. Nevertheless there is a continuing market for these essential materials and I am confident, as I know the industry itself is confident, that Canada will continue to be an important world supplier of strategic materials. This is due to continuing heavy world demand for the products concerned, to the steady depletion of many alternative sources outside this country and, even more important, to the fact that this country is a competitive producer.

As far as control of strategic materials during the period of critical shortage was concerned, we were able to keep formal controls to a minimum; and as soon as the supply situation warranted it, these controls were removed. We have, however, maintained a minimum framework of machinery which would enable us to reinstitute controls on materials on very short notice if it were necessary to do so.

On the procurement and production side, the program has made steady progress over the past two years. As I have pointed out on previous occasions, the rate of progress has varied, depending on the type of equipment or armament to be obtained for the armed forces. Because of long lead lines and the need for specialized facilities, it has taken longer to get into production on the more technical items. The over-all impact of the program on the Canadian economy has not been very great.

At the present time, defence procurement expenditures account for about 5 per cent of our gross national product. As far as individual industries are concerned, those whose capacity is most heavily engaged in defence production are shipbuilding, aircraft and, to a lesser extent, electronics, together with the main suppliers in each of these fields.

Looking at the present defence program, we find it is now apparent that we have reached the peak and that defence expenditures in the fiscal year 1953-54 will level off. This year will see more deliveries coming out of Canadian production than was the case previously. In the next year or two current plans will support a somewhat higher level of activity in the aircraft industry than in the past fiscal year, with more substantial increases in shipbuilding, electronics, and in the output of guns and ammunition. With regard to defence construction, the unusually 68108-308

Supply-Defence Production mild winter has made it possible to accomplish more than had been hoped for. As a result, there will be a very sharp reduction in the rate of expenditure on construction in the current fiscal year. Miscellaneous procurement, particularly in the clothing, textile and leatherwear fields, will continue to decrease.

Looking further ahead is obviously more difficult. This government-and I am sure all Canadians-cannot help but be encouraged by recent evidence that suggests a lessening in international tensions. But this government -and again I am equally certain all Canadians are in agreement-will wish to ensure that we do not allow these hopeful signs to distract us from the all-important job of building and maintaining our defences. We must, therefore, expect to keep up an effective level of preparedness for some years.

What, however, would our position be if we were plunged into another war? The possibilities for destruction in another major conflict are so horrible that it is difficult to estimate the probable course of hostilities. Nevertheless, we are continuing to make our preparations for the defence of this country. My colleague, the Minister of National Defence, has outlined'-to the extent that national security permits-the details of the plans of four chiefs of staff and how these plans are co-ordinated with those of our allies for the defence of North America and, indeed, the free world. It is my responsibility to ensure that Canadian industry is in a position to provide the support our armed forces will need. This is a serious responsibility, but again I am heartened by the ready response I have received from industry, both through individual companies and through industrial organizations. In this connection, I would like particularly to commend the Canadian industrial preparedness association.

I have already referred to the expansion and diversification that has taken place in our production of strategic materials. Our manufacturing output in real terms has more than doubled since 1939. Nearly two thousand new plants have been established and many new skills have been introduced to this country. We have, of course, paid special attention to those industries which make a direct contribution to the defence effort. We feel that we have now created, or are in the process of creating, the basic facilities necessary for the production of a large part of the modern and intricate equipment and armament that will be required by our armed forces.
Much of the basic capacity for supporting our defence effort has resulted from private

Supply-Defence Production industry's initiative and financing. In some instances the government has assisted by granting accelerated depreciation. Where necessary we have provided capital assistance to set up specialized capacity having little or no residual value. In these cases we have either created completely new facilities, or else we have provided specialized equipment or machine tools to companies having basic facilities and specialized know-how. In these cases, of course, title to the assets remains vested in the crown. As I have said, we have now completed most of our basic planning for specialized defence capacity and, for this reason, the capital assistance funds being requested in this year's estimates are essentially for the completion of projects started in previous years.
The Canadian economy, and particularly our defence-supporting sector, is, I feel, well equipped to play an immediate and decisive role in the event of an emergency.

On the other hand, if there should be a real improvement in the world situation, and we are all sincerely anxious that there will be, I am satisfied that the effects of such a development on our defence program would not seriously disrupt our economy. Over the past few years Canada has continued to make outstanding progress not only in further development of our natural resources but also in building up our economy on a strong and diversified industrial base. While the present defence effort has contributed to this progress, it has only been one contributing factor. As I have said before, the whole program was only a fraction of our total national production. A decrease in Canadian defence expenditures would, I feel sure, have no adverse effect on the Canadian economy as a whole.

The situation the government faces in the immediate future is, however, one of preparing for either of two eventualities-all-out war or an extended period of peace. From a production standpoint, this immediately raises the question of what facilities for producing weapons of war are to be kept in operation. For some items, it is comparatively easy to obtain them quickly out of normal commercial production. For the more complicated types of armament this is not possible and, as you know, it has been our policy over the past two years to build up a defence potential in certain lines as insurance against any emergency.

The maintenance of these specialized facilities, which have been set up to meet potential requirements of the armed forces, presents difficult problems. Canada is not, of course, alone in facing these difficulties. In the United States, too, the authorities are greatly

concerned. As a partial solution, we are studying the possibility of maintaining certain of our production lines operating at minimum economic rates by offering the end items to our NATO allies as part of our mutual aid commitments, and thus making another immediate and important contribution to the defence of the United Kingdom and western Europe. Of particular importance, from the viewpoint of defence, is the fact that a production line actually operating minimizes delays in supply and hence reduces the need for stockpiling. It is well known that, for storage and maintenance reasons, stockpiling is normally an expensive precaution, and equipment stockpiled is always liable to deterioration or obsolescence. We are hopeful that by supplying military equipment to NATO out of production we shall be able to keep our own production potential on a sound basis of readiness and, at the same time, assist our allies.

These are the main observations that I wish to make at this time. I am satisfied that the defence production and procurement programs are being satisfactorily implemented. The main orders have now been placed. Since the Department of Defence Production has been set up we have, in fact, placed about $3 billion worth of orders on behalf of our armed services. Deliveries on some of these orders have already been made. In the present fiscal year deliveries on items requiring a longer lead time will, for the most part, be completed by the end of March, with the exception of certain major items such as the CF-100 and the escort vessels, where the programs extend well into 1954 or even beyond.

In the course of getting the defence program under way, we have met with difficulties and experienced delays. We have, however, now resolved most of our problems. Our record of achievement is one of which we can be proud.

,Liberal,,Clarence Decatur Howe,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=1716566b-edef-40b2-9552-49510618c3bb&Language=E&Section=ALL

I propose in my remarks this afternoon to draw attention to some aspects of the achievements of this department, Mr. Chairman, and to call attention to certain matters which I think should engage the attention of this committee.
This department came into being on April 1, 1951. It has been in existence two years. So far as the estimates are concerned, the six items totalling this year $73 million do

As the minister has indicated, the department has made purchases on behalf of the government totalling some $3 billion, and the department has acted as agent not only for the Department of National Defence in many of the purchases, but also for foreign governments in the purchase of defence materials on their behalf.
The staff of the department on December 31, 1952, numbered 1,744. The estimates make provision for 1,784 persons on the staff of the department this year.

I would turn now to the annual report of the Department of Defence Production for 1952. Supply-Defence Production the ruling which I previously made. If I did not express myself clearly, I am sorry. My ruling is to this effect. The answers to questions such as the reason quantities of such and such a product were ordered, are not within the knowledge of the Minister of Defence Production. His department, as has been pointed out, is a purchasing agency. It purchases the quantities which it is required to do. Therefore the ruling I have made merely points out to the members of the house that the minister is not in a position to answer questions, nor are we on this item, in my opinion, in order when we discuss questions relating to quantities.

,Liberal,,William Alfred Robinson,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=3ada6e3a-9fea-4e2f-a739-b461030a41c3&Language=E&Section=ALL
1734544,ca.proc.d.1953-05-06.23.2.32.49,1953-05-06,5b04fb13-968f-4dac-80f6-3b569378e120,ca.m.5224,Mr. Fleming:,,LABOUR CONDITIONS,DEPARTMENT OF EXTERNAL AFFAIRS,DEPARTMENT OF DEFENCE PRODUCTION,Mr. Chairman, returns such as the one I hold in my hand, which come to the house as a result of questions being passed as orders for returns, according to the practice of the house are tabled by the Secretary of State. He derives his information from certain departments. In every instance this information came from the Department of Defence Production.

Now, I am not going to ask the Minister of Defence Production any questions about quantities. I am not proposing to do that at all. I accept these returns containing information which came from his department as being correct. I have no occasion to ask for any further information about quantities. I simply question, Mr. Chairman, whether when you come to the administration item for a department like this, the public of Canada should be called upon to bear the expense that is involved in this item to provide big staffs to make purchases in quantities like these, which I say cannot be justified. The quantities purchased are equivalent to 23 pairs of shoes per man in the Canadian armed forces in 21 months; 46 pairs of socks per man for 21 months; 17 handkerchiefs and 15 sets of winter underwear and 28 sets of summer underwear.

It is for purchases like these that we are being asked to provide funds for this department, so it may have at its disposal funds to carry on purchasing activities on such a scale. This is especially true in the face of the statement made by the Minister of Defence Production a half hour ago, drawing attention to the dangers and the expense of stockpiling. I think the minister has given his own condemnation of the policy reflected in this information that comes from his own department.

Having asked those questions as to what is being purchased, and having turned to that source of information for this partial answer, I come now to the question of where the purchases are made. I think it is a

Supply-Defence Production sound policy for this department, in making the huge purchases that it is making, that it should in the first place purchase in Canada where possible. In the second place it should purchase in the United Kingdom, being given value for our money, in order that we may assist the people of the United Kingdom in the face of their dollar shortage. This would enable Britain to buy more of our goods, because the curtailment of British purchases in this country, particularly of our agricultural surpluses, is undoubtedly due to the shortage of dollars. Here is a very good place for us to help provide them with the dollars, while helping ourselves in the matter of defence purchases and obtaining value for our money.
I think that, in the third place, purchases may then be made in the United States if we cannot purchase, first in Canada or second in the United Kingdom, goods to equal or almost equal advantage.
