There is another matter that arises in relation to this Department of Defence Production. The statute establishing this department, the Defence Production Act, chapter 4 of the statutes of 1951, makes provision in section 16 for the establishment of an account in the consolidated revenue fund to be known as the defence production revolving fund. Subsection 4 provides that expenditures charged to the defence production revolving fund shall not at any time exceed the receipts shown therein by more than $100 million or such further amount as parliament may authorize from time to time. On page 59 of the report of this department mention is made of the revolving fund. This revolving fund, as I take it, has been used to finance purchases of materials and commodities as well as in other ways.

In his statement this afternoon the minister reviewed some of the operations of this department in the field of direct purchases of materials in 1951 particularly, when there was keen competition for these materials. I should like to ask the minister-and I hope when he speaks further on these estimates he will give the committee a very full statement -the terms upon which these raw materials have been purchased and resold, because these commodities have been purchased, and then in part resold; but the public accounts indicate still a substantial net balance of purchases of these commodities as well as of goods directly related to the stream of armament production. We ask the minister for a very full report of purchases of that kind. Were they purchased by tender? That is a matter of some importance in relation to the safeguarding of the public treasury.

In that respect I should also remind the house that the same statute, by section 17, clothes the minister with power to make purchases in certain cases without tender. Section 17 of the act makes provision whereby the minister ""may, on behalf of His Majesty, enter into contracts'' with respect to the purchase of goods of the kinds described in sections 14 and 15 of the act. And paragraph (e) of section 17 provides-
A contract may be entered into by the minister without the approval of the governor in council if,

column2: in the opinion of the minister, the contract must be entered into immediately in the interests of defence,

column1: (ii)
column2: the estimated expenditure, loan or guarantee does not exceed twenty-five thousand dollars, or

column1: (iii)
column2: competitive tenders have been obtained and the lowest tender, involving an estimated expenditure not exceeding fifty thousand dollars, is accepted.

column1: It is clear that under those provisions if a contract is under $25,000 the minister, without any further authority from treasury board or from the governor in council, may make 68108-309i

Supply-Defence Production purchases without calling for tenders. In the case of contracts for amounts between $25,000 and $50,000, if he purchases without tender then he must have the approval of the governor in council.
Let me now refer to the annual report of the department where, at page 11, we will see that there has been something of a change in the system. That paragraph reads as follows:
The system under which contracts are awarded was altered during the year.
That is the calendar year 1952.

The minister's power to award contracts not exceeding $25,000, or $50,000 if competitive tenders have been obtained and the lowest tender accepted, remains unchanged. At the beginning of the year, contracts for larger amounts were subject to the approval of the governor in council but this was changed by order in council P.C. 3209 of May 30, 1952, and now, generally speaking, all contracts are approved by the treasury board where they are for sums larger than the minister can authorize.

Therefore we are left in this position, the minister in amounts up to $25,000 does not need to call for tenders and does not need any further approval, and as to amounts between $25,000 and $50,000 he requires approval, not by the governor in council but by treasury board, only if he purchases without tender.

Now, I think the time is past when power as broad as that in connection with purchases without tender should be left in the hands of a minister. We have seen in the defence expenditure committee what can happen when contracts are let without tender. There is no more important safeguard for the public treasury of Canada than that, save in the most insignificant amounts, purchases on public accounts should be made by tender, and that the invitation to submit tenders should be made widely known. Therefore I submit that the time has come when there should be some effective change made in the minister's powers in that respect.

And now in conclusion I come to one matter on which I wish there were time for extended debate, because the matter in question is of cardinal importance both to the public treasury and to the people of Canada. The report of the committee on defence expenditure came to this house only yesterday, within a matter of what may be only three or four days before prorogation. Part of that report, Mr. Chairman, relates to matters concerned with the Currie report, on which the committee was directed to conduct a study. Much of the time in committee, however, was devoted to a study of certain construction contracts carried out on behalf of the Department of National Defence by the Department of Defence Production and its
Supply-Defence Production creature, the crown corporation known as Defence Construction Limited.

In the report tabled in the house yesterday by the hon. member for Spadina, who was chairman of the committee, I have to say- and I am sorry to have to say it-that so far as it purports to review the operations that were disclosed in evidence before us, in terms such as these, in the third from last paragraph in the report-
The construction program in the face of a number of difficulties has been well conceived and carefully supervised and the public has received good value for its money-
-it just does not square with the facts. The report in that respect is a whitewash.

The Progressive Conservative members on the committee brought in an extended amendment to this report. As hon. members know, the rules of the house do not permit the filing of a minority report by a committee. The report a committee makes, according to our rules, can be only one report. The one tabled yesterday is, technically, the report of the committee. In actuality it is the report of the Liberal majority on the committee. And so far as it purports to sum up the evidence that was submitted to the committee in any sentence such as the one I have just quoted,
I say it is whitewash.

I wish to place beside that report this paragraph introduced by the Progressive Conservative members on that committee which deals with the activities of the Department of Defence Production and its creature, Defence Construction Limited, as contained in our amendment which was voted down in that committee yesterday morning, at its final session, by a government majority. I wish to read the five final paragraphs of the Progressive Conservative amendment. Preceding paragraphs of the amendment are, I say, directly relevant to questions before the house; but by reason of limitation of time I shall content myself with reading the paragraphs beginning with No. 7. They are as follows:

column2: From the outset your committee was hampered by a ruling which prevented the reception of evidence as to anything which occurred prior to March 31st, 1950, regardless of whether it might throw light on events subsequent to that date. In particular, your committee was thereby denied access to any reports made prior to that date concerning irregularities in relation to defence expenditures.

column1: It may be recalled that on March 16 the Prime Minister was compelled to admit the existence in government files of the MacNab report, made in 1949, which had been denied to your committee. This report, calling attention to the existence of conditions exactly similar to those found by Mr. Currie three years later, had been ignored by the government. The existence of this report establishes conclusively that the administrative breakdown preceded the outbreak of hostilities in Korea

in June, 1959, and that the government and the Department of National Defence have for a long period failed in the discharge of their responsibilities to safeguard public funds. Your committee therefore recommends that if such a committee should be appointed at any future session, it should be given powers of adequate breadth to carry on a comprehensive investigation.

column2: Your committee conducted a limited inquiry into construction work carried on by the Department of National Defence, and later on its behalf by the Department of Defence Production and its agent, Defence Construction Limited. Your committee was again impressed by the free and easy way in which large amounts of public money were spent. The many contracts awarded without tender, the many costly extras, the many contracts on a cost-plus basis, the many changes in plans and the many delays in completion have not been explained to the satisfaction of this committee. At Penhold, for instance, witnesses for the government departments sought to justify an expenditure of $25,000 on a speed-up, and equally to justify the abandonment of that speed-up program soon thereafter. Your committee has not been able to do more than scratch the surface of this subject in the limited time and with the limited opportunities at its disposal, and therefore recommends to the house that consideration should be given to undertaking a complete and impartial investigation into the construction program, including such matters as the construction of the R.C.A.F. station at Penhold, and including the awarding of the contracts, expenditures, delays in completion, and adequacy of the construction work performed, with power to retain such assistance from competent and independent engineers and contractors as may be considered necessary.

column1: That this committee recommend to the house that consideration should be given to retaining Mr. George S. What difference could two C.C.F. and one Social Credit vote have made in a committee made up of 17 Liberals out of a total membership of 26?

The fact of the matter is that the committee in this report has attempted to whitewash the government in this matter. The facts will not be hidden. It may be that a committee with a government majority of 17 as against 9 opposition members can carry a whitewashing report and defeat a Progressive Conservative amendment which stated the facts, but the committee in question is not the final court in this matter. It may be that this house with its overwhelming government majority will again seek to whitewash the government's record in this regard of profligate expenditure, of waste, of extravagance and of shocking inefficiency, but even that will not end this matter. This matter will be carried, whenever the government calls the time, to the people as the court of final appeal for an effective decision.

,Progressive Conservative,,Donald Methuen Fleming,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=5b04fb13-968f-4dac-80f6-3b569378e120&Language=E&Section=ALL
1734561,ca.proc.d.1953-05-06.23.2.32.66,1953-05-06,bb3f8499-7690-4f8e-a84d-e0729a45b283,ca.m.7200,Mr. Wright:,,LABOUR CONDITIONS,DEPARTMENT OF EXTERNAL AFFAIRS,DEPARTMENT OF DEFENCE PRODUCTION,Mr. Chairman, I should like to deal with this matter, but perhaps not at as great length as the hon. member for Eglin-ton. I think this is probably the most important department in the government today; at least it is spending the largest sums of money. Although its estimates this year are only $73,364,000 as compared with $123,452,000 last year, as the minister has stated, the department has spent approximately $3 billion of the Canadian taxpayers' money during the last two years and has purchased tremendous reserves of supplies and equipment for our armed forces.

When the hon. member for Eglinton was placing certain figures on the record with regard to the quantities of goods purchased and the prices paid, the minister indicated that we should be allowed only to discuss the prices of those goods, as that was the only thing in which he was interested. It would be nice if we could discuss intelligently the prices which the minister and his department paid for these goods, but I do not think we can when there is no indication as to the
Supply-Defence Production quality of the goods. That is a most vital matter.

The same situation obtained in the defence expenditures committee. We dealt with one item only, construction, and with only one part of the construction program, contracts. We were not able to go into the field and inspect the results of these contracts. One of the first things I sought when the committee met was that we should have some independent experts attached to it who could give us information as to whether the contracts which we were examining had actually been carried out in the field, whether the proper materials had been used and so on. A committee sitting here in Ottawa just could not perform that duty. Unless the committee had expert advice then I say that its work was not as efficient as it should be.

I am not saying that it was wasted, because we did get a lot of information from the departmental officials. We were all a lot wiser as to how contracts are let and the method of supervision used and so on, but the committee did not examine one thing in the field. We did not determine in one single case whether these contracts were actually being carried out efficiently and effectively as far as the construction was concerned.

I want to say that there was plenty of evidence that there were cases in which they might not have been carried out effectively and efficiently. I shall refer to only one or two small instances which the average person can grasp. At Penhold a valve was costing $44.85 used on a well. The particulars of this will be found at page 527 of the evidence. The well was drilled for 300 feet at a cost of $13,258. A small pumphouse 8x8 feet on a concrete foundation was built at a cost of $1,300.

Other schools were built under contract, and personally I think we failed to do a job in that committee. The committee was only able, as I said before, to deal with part of one item. We laid out a program when we started. We were going to look into armaments, tanks, ammunition, guns, small arms; naval vessels; operation Pine Tree; training costs of the service; recruiting costs; and soft goods-some of the goods which the hon. member for Eglinton was placing on the record this afternoon. The seventh item was military travelling costs. We spent too much time-several meetings-discussing the Currie report, something that had already been dealt with in the house and something on which I thought we were just wasting our time when discussing it in the committee.
I am not by any means satisfied with the results of the work of that committee; and

I do not believe the people of Canada will be satisfied after reading the report of the committee and the evidence that was placed before it, that the best possible job was done by the committee in seeing that the dollars we are spending on defence in this country are well spent. As I said before, the minister has indicated that we have purchased some $3 billion of goods. One of the things that should be done, and I moved this as a motion in the committee, is to see that the goods we are purchasing and stockpiling are actually being kept in proper condition, and that the goods we have bought and paid for are there.
In connection with the Currie report we had evidence that in some cases stocktaking had not taken place since the war, and in other cases not since 1947 and 1948. 1 moved in the committee:

Your committee recommends that parliament should ask the Auditor General to establish three teams of auditors, one for each branch of the service, navy, army and air force, to make such check audits of military establishments as are necessary to determine that proper stocktaking is being carried out and that proper records are being kept, also to determine the physical conditions of all stores and whether proper storage and maintenance methods are being followed, and that the Auditor General report the findings of these teams to parliament at regular intervals of not less than six months.

I think that is vitally important. What is happening to these goods we are stockpiling today? They are being placed in the various departments of national defence, the navy, army and air force, and each of those departments is drawing out of those stocks whatever goods they need for their day to day requirements. The only people checking those goods are those in the departments themselves. The chief auditors of the department report to the minister and, it is true, their reports are sent to the Auditor General. However, their first report is to the minister and then the report goes to the Auditor General.

I think it is vitally important that the goods we are stockpiling in Canada today should be under the control of parliament so we may know they are being properly preserved and that they will be available if an emergency should arise. I do not believe we know that today with the set-up we have in the Department of National Defence. I think the minister would agree that parliament itself should have a regular check on those millions and millions of dollars worth of goods that we are piling up in this country today. I think that is one of the things that the people of Canada are going to require.

1734580,ca.proc.d.1953-05-06.23.2.32.85,1953-05-06,bb3f8499-7690-4f8e-a84d-e0729a45b283,ca.m.7200,Mr. Wright:,,LABOUR CONDITIONS,DEPARTMENT OF EXTERNAL AFFAIRS,DEPARTMENT OF DEFENCE PRODUCTION,It is absolutely impossible for the Auditor General to check all the things that are in store in Canada. It is true that he may occasionally spot check, but that is all.

I am suggesting that the Auditor General, who is the servant of parliament and not of government, should be instructed to make more spot checks than are made at the present time. He should report directly to parliament at least twice a year, so that parliament itself will have assurance that these tremendous amounts of equipment, goods and raw materials are being properly stored; that they are not going to be drawn on by various departments of defence without any check by the Auditor General himself. I think that was a reasonable suggestion, but your committee turned it down.

I make the suggestion to the house, and I think every member of parliament has a responsibility in this. After all, we will pile up more of these goods. We have $3 billion worth already, and by the time we have completed our stockpiles we will probably have $4 billion or $5 billion worth of airplanes, tanks and other goods which might be required for immediate service. Until that is done I do not think we, as a parliament, are carrying out our duty to the taxpayers of this country.

I could go on at great length and deal with a lot of other things that are in the report. I do not suppose you, Mr. Chairman, will allow us to discuss the Currie report, which was a part of this report. It was shown in that report that, so far as the army works services were concerned, their stockpiling left much to be desired. When we suggested that we should have an examination into the stocktaking methods of the navy and the air force, we were turned down. We were told that the only things we could discuss were the items in the Currie report, the matters with which Mr. Currie himself had dealt. I do not think that is good enough. I believe parliament should have a direct check on those goods and services which we are putting in reserve today.

I believe that the defence expenditure committee should have expert advice to check on the contracts that are being let. They should be able to go into the field and check those buildings against the contracts that were let, thus determining whether or not we are actually getting value for the moneys we are spending. If that were done I am sure the taxpayers would feel a lot happier about the whole thing. I do not think they are

,Co-operative Commonwealth Federation (C.C.F.),,Percy Ellis Wright,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=bb3f8499-7690-4f8e-a84d-e0729a45b283&Language=E&Section=ALL
1734581,ca.proc.d.1953-05-06.23.2.32.86,1953-05-06,82878bc6-6bd2-407b-b2cc-7745aec02c2a,ca.m.8707,Mr. Macdonnell (Greenwood):,,LABOUR CONDITIONS,DEPARTMENT OF EXTERNAL AFFAIRS,DEPARTMENT OF DEFENCE PRODUCTION,Unfortunately, Mr. Chairman, I am not as well equipped as the member for Melfort, and I am not competent to discuss buildings. I do not propose to do that. But everyone likes to believe he has a little reservoir of common sense, and it does not seem to me that this matter of the business of the people of Canada has been conducted with common sense. I propose, therefore, to make a few observations on it.

Our present situation, of course, is an inheritance from the war. In wartime you have to spend money with very little check on it. Those of us who actually were in the forces know of the easy way in which everything there couid be covered by a return which said ""Destroyed by shellfire""; that covered everything. I think that, mutatis mutandis, the accounting was very easy at home, too.

When the new cold war came along we were asked to give, and I think rightly so, extraordinarily broad powers to the minister who had power during wartime. I am not going to take more than a second of your time, Mr. Chairman, to set out the powers that were given to the minister. He was given almost absolute power over the industry of Canada to make it lend itself to the necessities of defence. That was done with the approval of parliament, and I think we did the only thing we could.

So we slipped again into a situation where huge amounts were being spent, very much like wartime. We had the minister come and tell us what he was doing, assuring us that everything was all right. We had the Minister of National Defence, who is one of the world's great optimists, and he kept assuring us that everything was going along well. Still it was extraordinarily difficult to feel that you had any opinion at all, except that which was coming from those who were spending these huge amounts of money. The minister had done a lot of useful public work in wartime, and we were more or less in the position where we had very largely to take his word for things.
Then we all remember what happened at Petawawa a year ago. That incident blew up and the Minister of National Defence engaged the services of Mr. Currie, with the approval

of everyone. Then came the Currie report. When that came I said to myself, well now, at last we are going to have someone from the outside have a look at the whole situation. Surely we will not go along just accepting the situation blindly as in the past, and having no one from the outside look at it at all. Then I discovered to my amazement that it was proposed not to carry this investigation further. I found it very difficult to believe my ears. This course seemed to me to be directly opposed to what I call the dictates of common sense. If a manager of a large business found that a branch of one of his departments was not functioning well, he would do only one thing and that would be to extend the inquiry throughout the business.

As I say, things do not seem to work that way in politics. I am not a politician; I am just an enthusiastic amateur, and I have not full experience in these matters yet. As I say, it was very difficult for me to grasp the fact that we were going to be asked to act as we did. What we did do in parliament was to refer the report to the committee on defence expenditure, which was to examine all expenditures of public moneys for national defence and all commitments for expenditures for national defence. We were ordered by the house, first of all, to examine the Currie report, which was unnecessary because it spoke for itself. Then we went on to examine into other things. We now have the report to which the member for Eglinton has made reference.

What I want to put on the record, and what I wish I could shout into the ears of every citizen in Canada is that, of course, a committee of the House of Commons, conducted as it is now, is rather a queer affair. I do not want to use the words ""solemn farce"", though sometimes I thought it approached that. The committee was conducted with good temper and all the appearance of fairness to both sides. I mean we were allowed to ask questions, in fact we were really encouraged to ask questions. But all the time we suffered from one absolutely fatal disability, and that was that the evidence that wias coming to us was coming from government servants.

I want to be the last in the world to criticize faithful civil servants. But I put it to any sensible man that it is extraordinarily difficult for a man who has done a job to come along and admit there are any flaws in it. It is ten times more difficult when he is a public servant and knows that any admission on his part is not going to injure merely himself but is going to recoil on the head

of his political chief, and he cannot face the thought that anything of that sort should happen. In that committee we went through all the forms of what might be called a judicial inquiry, but in point of fact we were like a prosecutor who comes into court and is not allowed to have any witnesses of his own; he has only the witnesses for the defence. In addition to that, he is not allowed to have the expert assistance he has asked to have.

In the case of Penhold, where we made a somewhat broad inquiry, we asked-since we had been refused a general inquiry by Mr. Currie-to have him make an inquiry into this case. But no, that did not fit in, and it could not be had. It is rather interesting to go to the background of the committee and to realize how deeply ingrained these things are in the minds of the ministers. I want to read just a few words uttered by the Minister of National Defence when this thing came up. It shows the extent to which we have reached the stage where the government, copying the old French king, has said, ""The state, the state is us""-I suppose it should be ""we""; the state is the government and the welfare of the government is the welfare of the state.
This is what the minister said as recorded at page 1173 of Hansard for January 20, 1953:

But I hope the defence expenditure committee will be able to look into the report, have the officials of the department there and see whether the views I have already expressed on the cost of implementing some of the recommendations of the report are correct or whether the estimates of cost are as low as they can be made.

In other words, what the minister envisages, and what any other minister envisages, is that we ought to be good boys. We are to go into the committee and we are to have the representatives of the political chiefs there-with all respect to them, what else could they be-and we are to be guided by what they say. It is therefore not surprising that everything we asked for was turned down and that we reached the place where we are now.

What happened to us there, mutatis mutandis, reminds me a great deal of the kind of thing we hear about people who go to Russia. They go to Russia and they are taken around and are shown whatever is safe to be shown. They have no means of making any inquiry of their own; and if they are gullible people they come back and say that everything is all right. In a sense, that is what happened to us. We went into the committee. We had nobody of our own to whom we could appeal. The minister suggested that we should go to Penhold. It would have been an absolute waste of the minister's money if I had gone

Supply-Defence Production to Penhold. I am not an engineer, and I would have come back just as wise as when I went. In fact it would have been worse, because people would have said, ""You have been out to Penhold and you must talk no more because you have seen it for yourself.""

I think anything further I have to say, Mr. Chairman, can be said during the course of questions as they come along; but I want to make it clear-and this is the one point I wish to register-that we reached the stage where it was perfectly clear that things were not well. It was perfectly clear that the rather Pollyanna accounts that we got of everything were grossly exaggerated in the direction of optimism. Yet when it came to the point, the government absolutely insisted-and I say ""the government"" advisedly because this matter was voted on in the house-that the inquiry be not extended. In effect it was voted on before it ever went to the committee.

I say the government was absolutely unwilling to allow the inquiry to be extended. Does anyone out of the cradle, or even an intelligent child in the cradle, have any doubt as to why that was done? Would they have had any objection to having that done if they expected the result would be good? Therefore we reach the conclusion that the people of Canada, whose affairs have been found to be in an extremely bad state with respect to one part of this area of expenditure, are to be denied the obvious right which in any common-sense way of carrying on would be accorded to them, namely to have a full inquiry carried out by independent persons so they can be satisfied as to the situation. How can we reach any other conclusion?

As to this report which says that everything is all right, all I can say is that no one who has his ears open and goes about the country believes that is so. I have always discounted the criticisms that one hears; I have never accepted them lightly. But certainly since reading what Mr. Currie has had to say I have been much readier to accept them than I was before. As I said, there is no man inside or outside of the House of Commons but knows that in the matter of these huge expenditures there are irregularities, waste and inefficiency; and those are matters that should have been pursued in the only sensible way in which it can be done.

The time will come, I hope and believe, when the people of Canada will ask this question searchingly from those who have had it in their power to allow this common-sense thing to be done and have refused to do so.

,Progressive Conservative,,James MacKerras Macdonnell,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=82878bc6-6bd2-407b-b2cc-7745aec02c2a&Language=E&Section=ALL
1734582,ca.proc.d.1953-05-06.23.2.32.87,1953-05-06,a5d20b47-6869-470c-8621-982e467cd0dd,ca.m.9665,Mr. Pearkes:,,LABOUR CONDITIONS,DEPARTMENT OF EXTERNAL AFFAIRS,DEPARTMENT OF DEFENCE PRODUCTION,Mr. Chairman, other hon. members have referred to the limitations which were imposed upon the committee

Supply-Defence Production which was examining into defence expenditures, and I therefore do not intend to elaborate on those points this evening. I merely want to say that in that committee I had a feeling of frustration and disappointment because we had not been able to investigate as completely as I felt we should have been.

This evening I want just to touch briefly on one aspect of defence production. I want to ask the minister if he will explain the policy being followed with regard to the construction of naval vessels in this country, the distribution of the contracts in so far as the construction of those vessels is concerned, and to explain why there has been a lag in that production program and why it is not as far advanced as we had every right to expect it would be by this time.

As the minister knows, there are shipyards out on the west coast. From all the reports I have received those shipyards are not working to full capacity. A certain number of these new vessels have been constructed in the Vancouver, Victoria and Esquimalt yards; but the construction of those vessels has not proceeded as rapidly as was hoped. Good work has been done in the construction of those vessels, but the yards have been faced with considerable difficulties and obstacles.

Earlier this year it was brought to my attention that for all three vessels which were being constructed, all the castings were being made in eastern Canada, and that work was being held up in the Victoria yards because castings were not then available. In a letter I received from the Victoria joint shipyard council it was pointed out that the foundry of the Victoria Machinery Depot Company was one of the best in Canada and was quite capable of doing the work, but that the castings were being made in eastern Canada in spite of the fact that members of the staff of the Victoria Machinery Depot Company were being laid off.

I referred that matter to the minister's department, and the parliamentary assistant advised me that, in the interest of standardization and economy, it is generally necessary for particular components required for all vessels of the class to be prepared at one source, which would appear to be the reason these various castings were being made in eastern Canada and shipped out to the west coast when they became available in the east, though there might be delays on the vessels being constructed on the west coast.

But that does not seem to be a firm policy as far as the department is concerned. When the estimates of the Department of National Defence were under discussion I made inquiries as to why the second type of vessel, namely
TMr. Pearkes.]

the Crescent, which was being converted from a destroyer into one of the new escort vessels, had been given to a different yard than the one which had carried out the work on Algonquin, which was the pilot ship of that type. As reported at page 3991 of Hansard of April 16 the minister-I do not think it is necessary to quote his words-pointed out that it was usually the intention to spread the work around to different yards so that different personnel would be experienced in the work and would be able to carry on in a greater expansion program should it become necessary. I am paraphrasing, but I think that was the substance of his remarks.

If that is so with respect to the conversion of ships, should it not be tried in the production of component parts? When it is possible to produce component parts on the west coast, why is it necessary to have these component parts made in eastern Canada and shipped to the west?

I do want to emphasize the importance of keeping our shipyards and the government drydock at Esquimalt fully occupied. It is just as important to have trained personnel out on the west coast as in eastern Canada. I do not know whether any of the shipyards are being subsidized by the government. I presume that some form of subsidy may be given. If so, I wish the minister would explain that, and also tell me whether the delays have been due in part to the fact that civilian craft are being constructed in some of the shipyards, thereby causing a delay in the construction of naval vessels.

I understand that in some instances foreign countries have placed orders for freighters, and that penalty clauses have been included in the contracts for those freighters. If they are not completed by a certain time the shipyard will have a penalty imposed. If that is so and there are any penalty clauses -I understand there are none in so far as naval vessels are concerned-it is not unreasonable for the shipyard to take off many of its key personnel and place them on the freighter of the country which is imposing the penalty. That may be one of the causes of the delay. But as long as there are shipyards in the country which are not working to full capacity, surely it should be possible to make better progress with our naval construction program.

I put in a plea for our shipyards out on the west coast, and I hope the policy which the minister announced when he was speaking in the defence estimates debate will be applied and all yards in this country will be given full opportunity to work, whether on conversions or the construction of new vessels, or whether it is simply the production of

certain component parts which can be made in the different yards. I hope that the program will be distributed as much as possible. I do feel that it is just as important for us to proceed with our naval construction program as it is to keep on with the program for aircraft or any other branch of defence production.

,Progressive Conservative,,George Randolph Pearkes,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=a5d20b47-6869-470c-8621-982e467cd0dd&Language=E&Section=ALL
1734583,ca.proc.d.1953-05-06.23.2.32.88,1953-05-06,c638ba68-559c-40ce-ac85-82aa844a881c,ca.m.6448,Mr. McLure:,,LABOUR CONDITIONS,DEPARTMENT OF EXTERNAL AFFAIRS,DEPARTMENT OF DEFENCE PRODUCTION,I was not in at the beginning of this debate, but since coming in I have listened to a great many serious charges being made in reference to expenditures of the Department of Defence Production, and I am wondering how the minister will explain away these charges to the satisfaction of the committee.

I listened to the charges made by the hon. member for Melfort, and some of them seemed hard to believe. However, I want to say to the minister that I have a much more serious charge to make against his department. I refer to tne negligence of the department in not providing the machine shops at Charlottetown with more work than has been given to them. I charge the minister with overlooking our machine shops. Consequently they had little work to do on the repair of naval vessels and boats of different kinds. When that job was finished the minister forgot to give them any more. The result was that some 200 men have been laid off within the last few days. A telegram was sent to the Prime Minister by the city of Charlottetown, and no doubt the Minister of Defence Production knows what was in that telegram.

I do hope the minister will take care of the situation, because a large amount of money appears under different items in these estimates. Supply-Defence Production co-operation from the management, and everything I asked for was shown to me. As a member of that committee I had hoped they would be able to do so. In my opinion it was the greatest mistake that committee could make that those private corporations, in whose hands the tools of our defence rest, were not able to come before the committee and say: This is our problem of production. What happened when the report came down? It has been a whitewash report. But even if it was not a whitewash report, the committee did not do the job it was set up to do. It did not look into the business of the defence of the country. It did not look into the business of the production of arms. I repeat, it did not do the job it was set up to do and that it was proposed it should do, and that we had asked over and over again it should do.

Now I give the minister one question; that is the question of the design, production and development of aircraft in Canada. I will mention specifically the CF-100 and the CF-104 and the new flying saucer, which has been given such publicity in the press that it is no longer a matter of security. Mr. Chairman, there is one thing we can do to destroy the aircraft industry in Canada, and that is this. We can stop original design and original development by Canadians of aircraft designed for Canadian purposes. The CF-100, the jet liner and the Orenda engine were all Canadian-designed, all produced in

Canada. The reason their cost was as great as it was, and the delay was as great as it was, was that the aircraft company was not given its head and told to go on and produce these things, as were the aircraft companies at Wright held in the United States or at Farnborough in the United Kingdom, where the experimental stations were permitted to go ahead.

No, we had to interfere; we interfered at every conceivable stage with the A. V. Roe corporation. And today, Mr. Chairman, unless the A. V. Roe corporation can go ahead with the CF-100 and the future development of aircraft, we are going to find ourselves in a year or two behind the eight-ball, so far as aircraft production is concerned. You have to think two or three years ahead when you are producing aircraft; you have to have your design teams working two or three years ahead before you can go into production. That is the problem.

There seems to be considerable doubt whether our policy is to accept United States design, pay United States royalty and patent fees and destroy our own Canadian development, design and the originality of our own engineers. If we do that we put the clock back to where it was in the years prior to the second world war when no one, either in the United Kingdom or the United States, thought Canada could produce aircraft. We have proved that we can. We have proved not only that we can design them but that we can produce them as well as anybody in the world. That should be continued.

Let us look at this matter of naval ships. We are doing the same as we did prior to the first and second world wars. We are designing our armed forces to fight the last war. We are designing our navy as an antisubmarine navy, as though the submarine was all that we were going to have to fight. We have an anti-submarine job to do in some respects, but our principal job is to keep the sea lanes open. Our ships and our outlook toward design are based on 1939-45 thinking. Each bidder must satisfy himself by his own study of the plans, specifications and other contract documents by calculations and by personal inspection of the site respecting the conditions existing or likely to exist in connection with the execution of the work. Supply-Defence Production

In reply to a question by the hon. member for Kamloops, who asked whether Crown Assets Disposal Corporation had any condition in its sales order indicating that the purchasing people had to remove these slabs, an order was brought down which said this:
The sales order carried the following condition:

Requirement: Purchaser is required to either remove or demolish the building, removing all materials from the site, leaving it clean and tidy, levelling any excavations or mounds to the original contour of the ground to the satisfaction of a duly authorized representative of War Assets Corporation.

Surely, Mr. Chairman, the $5,000 which was spent for the removal of these slabs was not the responsibility of that department of government. It was in the first place the responsibility of the people who purchased these buildings from Crown Assets Disposal Corporation. When that was not done, it was the direct responsibility of the contractor who tendered for the erection of these buildings, as stated in the tender form.

One of the amazing speed-up actions taken by the department in this particular respect deals with the installation of the electrical distribution system. In order to speed things up the department allowed the Alexander Construction company to call for tenders for the supply and installation of that equipment. Then the department gave them a fee for their trouble, supposedly for the supervision of the installation and the trouble the company went to in calling for tenders. To refer to the first one, the construction program, just before we adjourn for tonight, now that the facts have been placed on the record by the hon. member for Wetaskiwin, it seems that the minister's assertion has been disproved completely. The sort of argument we are faced with, Mr. Chairman, when we try to analyse the attitude of the department and the actions of the department is summarized in the amendment moved by the Progressive Conservative members of the defence expenditure committee, as our suggestion of what should be in that report, where dealing with the activities of the department at Penhold and speaking of the speed-up to which the member for Wetaskiwin referred, we point out:
